title: What will it be like to referee Taylor v Pili?
description: Belfast's David Irving tells BBC Sport NI that being the man in the middle for Saturday's world title fight against Flora Pili will represent the fulfilment of a dream.
fullText:
When Katie Taylor steps into the ring at Croke Park in front of 80,000 fans for her world title fight with Flora Pili on Saturday night it will not just represent the fulfilment of a dream for the legendary Irish boxer.

For Belfast referee David Irving, who will be the man in the middle for the 27th and final professional bout of Taylor's decorated career, it will also be the realisation of a long-held ambition.

Taylor will aim to become a three-time undisputed world champion when she takes on Frenchwoman Flora Pili in Dublin.

The 40-year-old, who has won 25 professional fights and avenged her only defeat against Chantelle Cameron, will defend her light-welterweight WBO, WBA and IBF titles against Pili, who boasts an unbeaten 12-0 record.

With the vacant WBC title on the line, the Bray fighter has finally got her dream of boxing in front of a packed crowd at the Dublin venue.

But much focus will also centre on Irving, who regards taking charge of the contest as "right up there" with any of his previous assignments during more than 30 years as a referee.

"I can't believe that on Saturday night I'm going to be refereeing the biggest fight Ireland has ever seen. That is just amazing to try and understand," he told BBC Sport NI.

"It's an amazing honour to be recognised as an A-star referee, a world-class referee, to have people's confidence and support to referee such a big event.

"I'm thrilled, sometimes I still can't believe it. People come up to me and congratulate me and show me a lot of support.

"I've hoped that one day before I retire I would hopefully get a world title fight at home, with the WBC, and the dream has come true."

A former boxer himself with Holy Trinity in west Belfast, Irving's refereeing career has taken him around the globe, but being in charge of such a prestigious and historic fight in his native Ireland is a challenge that he is looking forward to hugely.

"I've been travelling the world since 2014 and I've always said I wish someone from Ireland would be up to that standard with the WBC," he added.

"I always said to myself wouldn't it be amazing to have someone that I could referee at home and lo and behold, Katie Taylor. She's an unbelievable ambassador for boxing and she opens herself up to everybody, not just in boxing.

"She has a great fanbase, she's a household name, north and south of Ireland, and to be part of that and to referee her I'm absolutely gobsmacked.

"In and out of the ring, she is such an icon."

Irving says he will go through a well established routine in his preparations for the big fight.

"A world title fight you make sure you have your uniform together, your pens, your scorecard, your towel and your water.

"You make sure you are hydrated because it could be a warm night and the fight could go the whole way, the whole 10 rounds, which can be very tiring.

"I'll be prepared, I always do a bit of training, always keep myself right eating wise.

"I can assure everyone that I'll be ready, no matter how big the fight is, how big of an occasion it will be, I'll be ready. I'm just looking forward to getting in there and I just hope it all goes according to plan."

The Belfast referee added that being prepared for all potential scenarios, including those that may not be anticipated, is all part of being fight-ready.

"It's the unexpected, being a referee. That part of me is always ready to go. That's where the confidence and the experience I have got now comes in, they have that confidence in me to make it an equal and smooth competition and may the best person win.

"You will be nervous, that's the thing about boxing, it's the unexpected.

"If you're a boxer, you go out to box, you have your programme in mind, you've done your work and you're ready to go.

"Refereeing is just the same. I've done my work, kept myself together, and do a lot of work, I do a lot of remote scoring, keep myself sharp, looking for the unexpected, and to be as quick as I can for the unexpected."

title: Barry-Murphy to be longest-serving Cardiff boss since Warnock
description: Brian Barry-Murphy takes charge of his 63rd game for Cardiff City when they face Portsmouth on Saturday.
fullText:
Brian Barry-Murphy will become Cardiff City's longest-serving boss since Neil Warnock on Saturday, 5 September.

The 48-year-old takes charge of his 63rd game as head coach when his side face Portsmouth at Fratton Park.

In doing so, he signifies the longest period of stability since Warnock departed the Welsh club seven years ago.

Barry-Murphy will surpass the total number of matches overseen by Neil Harris between November 2019 and January 2021.

It says a lot about Cardiff's recent managerial turbulence that the Irishman will claim this accolade after less than 450 days in charge.

He is the eighth permanent appointment - and the 10th when including caretaker bosses - to take charge at Cardiff since Warnock left in November 2019.

One person who will not get carried away by the accolade is Barry-Murphy himself. By his own admission, he is not one to reflect when there is work to be done.

"It's a great privilege to be at a club of this size and backed by so many incredible supporters. But I don't look back too often," the former Manchester City academy coach admitted when told about the milestone.

"I'm very focused on the now and trying to give the supporters more nights they can enjoy and less like [Wednesday's defeat to QPR]."

Cardiff can reach Championship play-offs - Bielik

Lawlor set to miss Wales' Nations League games

Barry-Murphy took the reins at Cardiff during a difficult period for the club after their first relegation to the third tier in 22 years.

The former Rochdale manager exceeded the average 277-day tenure of his predecessors by March of this year, when the Bluebirds were second in League One.

And like Warnock he delivered a promotion, although his came in the first season, to get Cardiff back into the Championship at the first attempt.

Average attendances for home games increased in League One - despite relegation the previous season - and will likely do so again this campaign.

The emergence of several talented youngsters and the style of play adopted during his spell has rejuvenated the feeling among Cardiff fans.

And after three draws and a defeat to start the campaign, the question now is whether he can maintain the positive feeling in the Championship.

Barry-Murphy is confident of it, even after a quiet transfer deadline day, during which Cardiff were unable to sign the targets their head coach wanted.

Many fans have voiced their concern about a lack of squad depth, with only four players recruited at the Cardiff City Stadium this summer.

But Barry-Murphy feels he has been backed in the transfer window and is pleased with the players at his disposal for a gruelling Championship season.

There would be no better way for the Irishman to mark his latest Bluebirds achievement than to claim his first Championship win on Saturday.

title: Is Hearts' McPake poised to gatecrash Pocognoli's Scotland squad?
description: Josh McPake has made a significant impact since joining Hearts. Could he now do the same for the Scotland national team?
fullText:
On the eve of the Scottish FA's highly-anticipated summit on youth development in Scotland, one of the country's own stole the show in a thrilling Edinburgh derby.

And as it happened, the new national team head coach, Sebastien Pocognoli, was in the Easter Road stands as Josh McPake spearheaded Hearts' entertaining victory over Hibernian.

Even before the Belgian was appointed, there were some calls from the Tartan Army to include the 25-year-old winger, such has been his emphatic start to life in Gorgie since making the switch from St Johnstone in the summer.

The clamour for his inclusion is now becoming inescapable.

A Rangers youth product, the question hanging over McPake since signing his pre-contract with Hearts in January, was could he cut it among the big boys.

Under the lights in Leith, McPake waltzed through the weak Hibs backline before bending a beautiful effort beyond Raphael Sallinger - with a deflection off Grant Hanley - sparking bedlam among the travelling supporters behind the goal.

The talk of the toon are the boys in maroon, but the chat in all corners of the country is about McPake. He really is the man of the moment.

In eight games, he has registered two goals and four assists for an increasingly easy-on-the-eye Hearts side, who are emerging as contenders for the campaign's great entertainers.

In the first 30 minutes at the home of their city rivals, they were magnificent. McPake - along with fellow Scotland hopeful Calvin Miller - was unplayable, hugging the touchline and leaving home full-back Felix Passlack for dust.

He destroyed the former Borussia Dortmund defender before teeing up James Wilson's opener, with former Hearts striker Ryan Stevenson explaining that was the perfect example of how much of a handful he is.

"It is so hard for defenders when wingers play on the opposite side," Stevenson said on Sportsound. "They always want to come on the inside, but he is happy to go on the outside and feint and go on his left side.

"One of his biggest attributes is you don't know which way he will go."

That was evident again when McPake took a stroll for his superb solo goal, one he was desperate for in his first derby.

"I thought we started the game really, really well," McPake told BBC Sport Scotland. "Obviously, I got the assist in the first half, but I really, really wanted the goal."

While he was happy to admit his desire to get on the scoresheet, the winger was a little more reluctant to indulge in any Scotland call-up conversation.

As understandable and mature as that may be, it won't stop the rest of us doing so. But McPake is more reserved than most because of his tricky route to the top.

After coming through the Rangers ranks, he was sent out on loan six times, before finally settling at Stirling Albion in League 1.

Impressing, he caught the eye of St Johnstone, albeit he was initially involved in their top-flight relegation.

It was in the second-tier last term where McPake started to shine. Head and shoulders above the rest, Derek McInnes' Hearts secured his services on a pre-contract. Then McInnes left Tynecastle for Ibrox.

"These things happen in football," explained McPake, who couldn't hide his appreciation for Vrancken.

Are Hearts derby heroes ready for Scotland?

That feeling is reciprocated. Even if the attacker was left out of Hearts initial European squad.

"It was a difficult start and he had to adapt in several ways and the things we wanted to see and be decisive in certain moments," the head coach said.

"But he did great and picked up those things and he is really strong in defence as well as offence and I'm pleased to see this happening."

And it appears Vrancken isn't the only one, with the winger dominating much of the post-match discussions.

"I know he has had loan moves, but it is about getting the right environment and the right manager," former Hibs midfielder Scott Allan said on Sportsound.

"Now he has landed with Wouter Vrancken and I think he will be a manager who will enhance his career.

"When they get him isolated, he puts defenders under pressure.

"I wouldn't be surprised if he is named in the next Scotland squad because he is the standout at present."

While McPake might be the standout, he has a more than decent support act.

Fellow forwards Miller and Wilson are in the mix for involvement in the upcoming Nations League games this month, too.

Teenager Wilson has already been capped, but since spending the second half of last season on loan with Tottenham Hotspur's under-21 side, he has taken his game up a notch.

His second derby goal at Easter Road will have done his hopes of a national team return no harm - nor will his wonderstrike against Rapid Vienna - with Stevenson adding he showed "total striker's instinct".

"We have to come to the point with a new manager coming in for Scotland, there is room to bring in a bit of freshness," he added.

Not dominating the discourse as much as last week for his heroics in Austria, hirpling into the box to score in extra-time and force penalties before netting his own, Miller strengthened his case yet again for an impressive performance.

He was spoken off in some circles as an outside shout for a World Cup spot following his superb Falkirk form, but that always seemed too much of a stretch.

But now, he and his team-mates are front and centre, catching the eye of everyone watching. Mr Pocognoli, are you watching?

title: Who are best Man City players to buy? FPL gameweek three dilemmas
description: BBC Sport FPL expert Gianni Buttice looks at some of the biggest dilemmas facing Fantasy Premier League managers heading into gameweek three.
fullText:
BBC Sport's FPL expert Gianni Buttice looks at some of the biggest dilemmas facing Fantasy Premier League managers heading into gameweek three.

If you do not own Erling Haaland (£15.5m), using a chip to bring him in is much simpler than spending several transfers to fit in the game's most expensive player.

A Wildcard lets you move quickly on trending players, improve team value, and invest heavily in two sides you may not have much exposure to in Manchester City and Chelsea, who face Coventry and Hull at home over the next fortnight.

The Free Hit chip also has an upside, allowing you to avoid the Arsenal versus Chelsea fixture and consider players from Brighton, Newcastle, and Brentford.

If you are not using a Wildcard or Free Hit, choosing Haaland as your Triple Captain looks a strong option, which I am likely to run with.

Coventry have been among the most defensively vulnerable sides and Manchester City impressed last time out, while their Norway striker has had a clear midweek before Saturday's game at Etihad Stadium.

City also host Ipswich in gameweek seven and Hull in gameweek 16, but both fixtures fall during heavy Champions League congestion.

Bruno Fernandes (£12.0m) faces Coventry at Old Trafford in gameweek 14, although that also comes in a run of three matches in seven days.

Rayan Cherki (£7.7m) is this week's most-bought player, with two price rises already. After his impressive last outing, he is the standout midfield pick.

Phil Foden (£7.0m) is also worth considering, with stronger underlying expected data than Cherki over the first two games, while Elliot Anderson (£6.4m) looks a solid long-term hold.

Cherki and Foden may become minutes risks later in the season, especially after the deadline-day signing of Enzo Fernández (£6.9m). In defence, Josko Gvardiol (£5.6m) is the best option.

The half-time substitution of Christos Tzolis against Aston Villa was a concern for owners.

We saw in gameweek one how dangerous he can be and many expect him to be first choice this season, albeit subject to early substitutions.

He's far from a hard sell though and arguably a comfortable hold at £6.5m.

Manchester United captain Fernandes is close to the ideal FPL asset: talismanic, takes set-pieces, rarely injured or substituted, and a reliable scorer.

He is a stronger option than Cole Palmer (£9.6m) or Bukayo Saka (£9.5m), but he is also significantly more expensive.

Because captaincy is so important, look ahead. if you are unlikely to captain Fernandes soon, but would give the armband to Palmer or Saka, the switch is worth considering.

It's also worth noting there are plenty of other good assets at Chelsea and Arsenal, whereas Fernandes is in a league of his own at United.

It is easy to be tempted by a new signing, but I would wait at least a week before buying anyone who has only just joined.

Most are unlikely to start this weekend and may be limited to cameo appearances. If they impress on debut, you can react then.

To name a few, I will be closely monitoring Daniel Munoz (£5.4m), Bradley Barcola (£8.0m), Jack Grealish (£6.5m), and the impact Fernandez will have on the minutes of other Manchester City midfielders.

title: How Motherwell's blueprint is defying second-season syndrome
description: New faces, same identity. Motherwell's approach has fans dreaming of a campaign that surpasses the highs of 2025-26.
fullText:
Motherwell secure a place in Europe and serve up the best football their fanbase has ever experienced - but at what cost?

They lose their transformational manager after just a year in charge and have the spine ripped out of their team.

So then arrives an unknown face in the dugout, 35-year-old Alfred Johansson, and 11 new players.

Supporters of provincial sides have long been conditioned into fearing second-season syndrome after enjoying a year of fun but Motherwell continue to defy traditional Scottish football thinking.

Now supporters of the fan-owned Fir Park club are dreaming of a campaign that surpasses the highs of 2025-26.

Motherwell demolish 10-man Dundee Utd to extend unbeaten start

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

It is difficult to comprehend how one man can influence one club over such a short period of time, but the impact of Jens Berthel Askou, now head coach of Toulouse in Ligue 1, has gone beyond Lanarkshire.

In relation to what can be achieved in Scotland on a modest budget, Dundee United boss Jim Goodwin said the Dane's work in the Scottish Premiership has given "guys like myself a bit of a wake-up call".

Goodwin's 10-man side were pulled apart by Johansson's iteration of Motherwell on Wednesday, extending their unbeaten league start after four games, but a noticeable shift in United's style has clearly been inspired by Askou.

There has been no style shift at Fir Park, though. No matter the coach, no matter the players, the club now have an identity that has been responsible for a huge spike in attendances, as well as the on-field results.

Speaking at an event for the Well Society, Motherwell's 4,000-strong fan-ownership group, vice-captain Stephen O'Donnell detailed how the club's continuity has benefited the squad.

"If the new manager was a 'heid it and kick it' manager, we'd all be in a right pickle," the defender said. "I definitely wouldn't be playing centre-back anymore."

Out of Askou's first-choice XI last term, only four have started a Premiership game this season, whether that is through players departing or injuries.

Goalkeeper Calum Ward and centre-back pairing Stephen Welsh and Paul McGinn were fundamental to the club setting a new clean-sheet milestone and achieving the second-best defensive record in their top-flight history.

Ward left for Queens Park Rangers, McGinn is recovering from long-term injury, and Welsh is now at Championship leaders Swansea with Elijah Just, who became Motherwell's top transfer sale in July, just a year after Udinese's Lennon Miller had set the previous record.

Elliot Watt, arguably the Premiership's standout midfielder last term, also exited for Samsunspor in Turkey, while Callum Slattery left for Sheffield Wednesday after his contract expired.

Motherwell are providing a blueprint for other Scottish sides following an unprecedented period of transfer income totalling more than £10m across the past year.

That seems to have opened the door for the club to shop in a better market this summer but there is also now enough evidence for players joining to know the future rewards that can come with impressing at Fir Park.

Midfielder Joe Hodge, regarded as the Watt replacement, was playing in Portugal's top flight last term and centre-back Martin Moormann was playing in the Austrian Bundesliga, while reported six-figure signing Jardell Kanga will hope to fill the void left by World Cup breakout star Just.

Even the appointment of Johansson was eye-catching given his previous, and only, job in management was a two-and-a-half-year spell at 26-time Norwegian title winners Rosenborg.

And the early indicators are hugely encouraging. The Swede is showing signs he can take last season's fringe players to a new level while finally unlocking the potential of Rangers academy graduate Alex Lowry, who will return to Ibrox on Saturday.

Granted, it has not all been perfect.

Motherwell will need to deal with the fact they have not won major silverware since 1991 for at least another eight months after a rotated side suffered a shock League Cup defeat at second-tier Stenhousemuir.

A manic 3-3 draw against St Mirren, during which Johansson's men conceded three times in the space of 10 minutes, came following a hectic and ultimately unsuccessful Conference League qualification attempt that still provided memorable moments against HB Torshavn, HJK Helsinki and Freiburg.

With eight points from four league fixtures, their tally for this season is already double what it was last term at this stage.

It took until late September for Motherwell to get their first Premiership win under Askou last year while they worked through teething issues.

Those 12 months under the Dane meant Johansson took over a squad already ingrained in playing in the way he sees the game but what has he actually changed?

To the eye, not a lot. The former Copenhagen youth coach said he only wanted to tweak the cogs in a well-oiled machine when he was appointed.

Motherwell are more or less still playing with a fluid 4-4-2 formation in and out of possession, with rotations remaining an integral part of their approach.

One difference fans were quick to notice, though, was Johansson's team playing with more width and more intensity on the ball, with crosses from wide areas becoming more frequent as marauding left-back Emmanuel Longelo's influence grows after an excellent debut season in Scotland.

The sample size under the young Swedish manager is still small in comparison to Askou's, but average possession is almost identical, just below the 60% mark.

At this early stage, the data says Johansson's side are scoring, shooting and passing more, but Askou's freakish defensive numbers will take some beating.

Next up for the thriving Lanarkshire club is a short hop to Ibrox on Saturday (15:00 BST), where they have won in three of their past four visits.

That a once-dreaded trip is now relished says it all about the mood around Motherwell.

title: Pato consortium's Northampton investment approved
description: The Independent Football Regulator approves investment into the Cobblers by a Brazilian consortium.
fullText:
A consortium including former AC Milan, Chelsea and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato has had a "proposed shareholding aquisition" of Northampton Town approved by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) and English Football League (EFL), the League Two club has said.

Sports Alpha Capital (SAC) was previously in discussions about taking over Colchester United earlier this year but decided to pull out of a potential deal following initial talks.

Pato is named by SAC, external as one of its investors, along with Gemcorp Capital, a London-based independent investment management firm.

The size of SAC's proposed shareholding in the Cobblers has not been disclosed at this stage.

The club said that full details regarding the investment, structure and the principal investors involved would be announced upon completion of the deal.

Friday's announcement ended months of speculation, after the club first disclosed it was talking to the "well-funded investment group" in April.

Pato, 37, retired from playing last year. He is best known for his five-and-a-half-year spell at AC Milan where he scored 63 goals in 150 matches and won the Serie A title in the 2010-11 season.

Northampton chairman Kelvin Thomas said: "This has been a detailed and rigorous process, involving significant scrutiny of the proposed investment, the ownership structure, financial sustainability, and the suitability and financial standing of those involved.

"The successful completion of both the IFR and EFL processes represents an important milestone for the club and should provide supporters and stakeholders with further confidence in the proposed investment and the foundations being put in place for the club's future.

"We would like to thank both the EFL and the IFR for their professionalism, diligence and thoroughness throughout their respective processes.

"As supporters will see from their varied backgrounds, there is a genuine passion for football within the group. A number of the investors have already visited Northampton, spent time at the club and attended matches.

"They will bring a strong blend of football, corporate and financial expertise to the club and with significant Brazilian representation within the group we also hope they might bring a little Brazilian excitement and flair with them.

"Now the regulatory processes have been completed we move towards completing the remaining documentation and finalising the investment. Full details regarding the investment, structure and the principal investors involved will be announced upon completion.

"We thank the fans for their patience, but it is reassuring that these in-depth processes are in place for football."

The deal comes after a difficult year for the League Two side.

The Cobblers suffered relegation to the fourth tier last season, finishing bottom of the League One table. They remain without a win so far in 2026-27.

In April, the club announced a pre-tax loss just short of £3m, with Thomas previously saying that the proposed investment would make the club debt-free.

Northampton appointed Chris Hogg as their manager in May and brought in 13 players during the summer transfer window, including striker Matty Warhurst from Manchester City.

title: The handcyclist and model grabbing every opportunity after paralysis
description: Meet Callum Russell, the Great Britain handcyclist and model proving there can be "an amazing life after injury".
fullText:
"I remember everything about that day. I knew straight away that I'd broken my back."

In 2018, Callum Russell had just started making a living out of mountain bike racing. He had a new sponsor and was excited to race at Gisburn Forest. He knew every twist and turn of the course.

But on a practice run he misjudged a jump and, as he crashed to the ground, he knew it was serious. He couldn't feel his legs and, as he was airlifted to hospital, he was certain his life had changed forever - but he also knew, even in that moment, that he would adapt.

"I genuinely didn't have that moment of trauma. There was the realisation that it's going to be hard, I'm going to have to relearn things, but that's what we're moving on to," Russell, 30, tells BBC Sport.

"I never at any point had a moment of a breakdown or anything like that."

When he came round from surgery Russell learned he had severed his spine at T11, in the middle of his back, and he was paralysed from the waist down.

"The realisation dawns that you're going to have limited bladder control, bowel function, and you're going to have to learn to use a wheelchair full-time," he said.

But within weeks, with the support of family and friends, he was back outside.

"It was the first thing I wanted, to get outdoors. I want to feel physically fit, so how am I going to do that?"

The answer, initially, wasn't cycling. His first attempt on a handbike wasn't enjoyable because it felt so different from his beloved mountain biking.

"I wasn't in the mindset to do that. I just thought 'I'm going to close the door on that, and I don't ever need to do it again'," he said.

Rowing, though, as a sport he had never tried before, gave him a new sense of freedom. He quickly progressed to Great Britain's Para-rowing squad, winning a bronze on his international debut at a World Cup in 2022.

But it was during a training camp that he saw one of his team-mates, Paralympic and world champion Ben Pritchard, using a handcycle to ride around the lake after they had finished training. His interest in cycling was rekindled.

Russell switched sports in 2023, and two years later made history as the first British male handcyclist to win a World Championship medal with his time trial bronze in Belgium.

"I always say that rowing gave me what I needed from sport, in terms of fitness, but not necessarily what I loved from sport - just being able to go out the door and be independent and explore," said Russell, who is from Stockport.

"[Winning] was an amazing feeling, and I'd like to think that I was able to celebrate that with the other handcyclists as a bit of a team effort, and not just off my own back.

"I had family and everyone there, so it was a real realisation that this could be something."

In Alabama this weekend, Russell will return to the World Championships as one of Great Britain's medal hopes.

And while as a UK Sport-funded athlete, cycling is Russell's number one focus, he supplements his income with modelling jobs on the side.

Signed to a talent agency, who he first met not long after his accident when he decided to attend a casting on a whim, he has appeared in television adverts and worked with numerous well-known brands.

"I would say I'm quite reserved, and I'm probably always the one that just observes, sits back and watches the situation, but there's definitely situations where I would never have tried before, or opportunities that I would never have tried before my injury, because I'd have just thought that's not for me," he said.

"Whereas now, it's sort of like why is that not for me?

"Something's happened to me that's pretty unique, and so why should I not go and try other opportunities that you never know what will come from it."

Reflecting on his injury, he added: "I think that there is definitely an amazing life after injury. There's no doubt that it will change your life, and there's huge learning curves there, but there's also massive amounts of opportunities that maybe you wouldn't have before that injury, so it's definitely worth just grabbing them with both hands and going for it."

title: 'I haven't delivered' - MVP set for final bout on UFC contract
description: Michael 'Venom' Page says he needs to remind the UFC why they signed him, with his contract set to end after his UFC Paris bout on Saturday.
fullText:
Michael 'Venom' Page will fight the final bout on his UFC contract when he takes on Nursulton Ruziboev in Paris on Saturday.

The 39-year-old has had a mixed career in the octagon since joining in 2024, with four wins from five fights - and all his victories by decision.

Known for his eye-catching striking, MVP admits he has underperformed in his UFC tenure without a stoppage to his name.

"I'm still buzzing to be in this game, but then there's also [the fact] I feel like I haven't delivered what I wanted to deliver," Page said.

"We (Page and the UFC) don't seem to be as aligned as I thought we would be.

"Maybe at the beginning I felt like we were - something's changed. But either way, the goal is [to] keep stepping out there and kicking people in the face.

"[This fight is to] specifically to remind the UFC why they brought me to this organisation."

Page has openly spoken about his frustration about the frequency of his fights, questioning why the UFC were not booking him more regularly.

The Englishman has fought twice at middleweight – beating Sharabutdin Magomedov and Jared Cannonier - despite being a seasoned welterweight.

An all-British bout with Leon Edwards has also not materialised.

Page faces a tough opponent in Ruziboev, who arrived in the UFC in 2024 with 20 submissions, has competed in 50 MMA fights and has four stoppages in his five victories in the octagon, with one defeat.

Uzbekistan's Ruziboev, 32, is the underdog against the more experienced Page, who is back at middleweight again for this bout.

With Page set to enter free agency, he would represent an attractive option for several rival promotions having spent most of his MMA career with Bellator.

But the Londoner is keen to sit down with the UFC after Saturday.

"This fight is important to re-establish myself with the UFC," Page said.

"Then sit down with them and say 'OK, guys, can I have an idea of what you expect of me? Can I have an idea of what direction is best for me to work towards? Can I have an idea of what it is that you guys need from me?'

"And then we get to work... I prefer if I have targets, and I have an idea of what I'm supposed to do, then I go and attack it."

title: Earps eyes Man Utd reunion as WSL comeback nears
description: Mary Earps is back in the Women's Super League and hopes to mark her return by facing former club Manchester United.
fullText:
Mary Earps is no stranger to the Women's Super League and hopes to mark her return with a match against her former club.

The new London City Lionesses goalkeeper felt it was "meant to be" that her potential debut could come against Manchester United.

During the peak of her career, she spent five seasons at United, becoming England number one and twice being named Fifa's goalkeeper of the year.

After a spell at Paris St-Germain, Earps wants to return to England on a high in Friday's season opener (19:00 BST) and will no doubt find herself in the limelight again.

"I got a nice reception at Old Trafford [in the Women's Champions League last season] and it meant a great deal to me at that time," Earps told BBC Sport.

"United has changed a lot since I left, but I spent five wonderful years there and I made amazing memories.

"I won an FA Cup and met a lot of incredible people. I know the fans don't change - they are still as hardcore as ever."

The 33-year-old made more than 100 appearances for United and helped them win their first major trophy in 2024.

She also played a crucial role in England's victory at Euro 2022 and their route to the 2023 World Cup final while she was at United.

That earned her many individual accolades, including BBC Sports Personality of the Year in 2023 and she became one of the country's most recognised and influential players.

However last November, her book caused controversy and dominated headlines in the media for several weeks.

Even so, Earps received a warm applause when she faced United with PSG last season and the mural painted of her outside Old Trafford remains.

As she prepares to face her former club again, what does Earps want to achieve at London City and why was it time to return home?

Earps spent two years at PSG and made 22 appearances in the Premiere Ligue last season.

She left United in search of Champions League football and silverware, but was also able to take a break from the limelight in England.

That attention rose again last year following the release of her book, but Earps is thankful for the experiences she gained in Paris.

"I'm grateful for all the amazing love and support that I've had over the years, but it was nice to be away," said Earps.

"PSG is a great club. Getting to experience the Parc des Princes, the French food, the Parisian way of life and the language - I think it was good for me.

"I'm an intense person, especially when I'm on the pitch, so it was good for me to be able to take a period of reflection away from the craziness in England.

"But that being said, I'm incredibly grateful for this platform that I've been given so it's not a complaint. I went away to push myself out of my comfort zone."

However, upon the expiry of her contract, Earps craved a return to England where she could experience WSL atmospheres once again.

"Of course, there's always things that you miss. I'm very, very happy to be home," she added.

"I missed the English football culture - the way you feel when you walk into a stadium, the electricity of the crowd, the feeling around women's football in this country.

"I knew I was probably going to miss that going away which is why I'm so excited to be back. Distance makes the heart grow fonder."

Earps is one of the big-name players to join London City this summer, joining two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and Spain defender Mapi Leon at the club.

She started both of London City's past two pre-season matches but knows she faces a battle to take the number-one shirt given fellow goalkeeper Elene Lete impressed last term.

"The reality of it is that I've been here a few weeks and I'm trying to earn my place in the team every single day," said Earps.

"Elene did a great job last year and it won't be easy between us to see who starts. I think that is another great thing about being part of a fantastic squad.

"I just want to contribute to the team's success and hopefully that is playing a lot of games and being a part of their history in some small way."

Earps announced her international retirement in 2025 but does not intend to call quits on her club career any time soon.

She signed a two-year deal with London City and believes she can still improve as the club plots a course up the WSL table.

"I want to continue to play at the highest level, to win at the highest level for as long as possible and to be a part of something special," said Earps.

"I really do believe that London City will go on to do great things for a long time. They want to be the best in class and world-leading.

"That is something that I'm always pushing to be - to be the best version of myself as a player and a person every day.

"It's a great place to be for me to max out on whatever potential I have left. The moment that I don't think I can learn any more, I won't continue to play.

"I still feel like I've got a lot to give and hopefully there's some fantastic days around the corner. I'm really looking forward to this chapter."

title: From playing with Rashford to non-league and new career
description: Ten years after lining up with Marcus Rashford for Manchester United, Joe Riley tells BBC Sport about his new career - and why he does not miss full-time football.
fullText:
A Tuesday night in Workington in late August and Joe Riley leads his Warrington Rylands team-mates out for a match at the Fibrus Community Stadium in the seventh tier of English football.

Rylands race into a 2-0 lead in Cumbria before losing 3-2 after having two players sent off in a chaotic Northern Premier League Premier Division encounter played in front of 638 supporters.

"A few years back I wouldn't speak for 24 hours if I lost," says Riley, whose side host Hyde United in the first qualifying round of the FA Cup on Saturday (15:00 BST).

"Now if we lose, it's not ideal, but there's always another game around the corner."

It is 10 years since Riley, then aged 19, started at left-back for injury-hit Manchester United against Danish side Midtjylland in the Europa League at Old Trafford, the same match Marcus Rashford also made his first start for the club.

While Rashford has gone on to rack up more than 400 club appearances and earn 78 England caps since scoring two in that emphatic 5-1 win, external a decade ago, Riley left United at 21 with two first-team appearances to his name - and drifted down the leagues after bad luck with injuries.

While recovering from one injury too many at League Two Walsall, he started studying for a new career.

Now aged 29, he sells life insurance, income protection, critical illness and injury cover as a financial protection advisor - while playing non-league football.

"I lived with Scott McTominay for six years, and Marcus and I also came through the academy together," Riley tells BBC Sport.

"These people were like family to me.

"Of course I would have liked to have played more games for United but things didn't work out like that.

"I don't dwell on the past - I'm just happy that it happened. I've now got my foot in the door for the next chapter of my life. I'm progressing with another career that's setting me up for the rest of my life."

Riley grew up in Lytham, Lancashire, and joined United at the age of six.

He went on to play for the under-18s with Rashford, Scotland midfielder McTominay, now at Napoli, and England goalkeeper Dean Henderson, who is at Crystal Palace.

It was while Riley was playing regularly for the under-21s, aged 19, that he - and 18-year-old Rashford - got their big break in February 2016 under Louis van Gaal.

Having come on as a substitute in a 3-0 win at Shrewsbury Town in the fifth round of the FA Cup three days earlier, Riley was named in the starting line-up for a Europa League last-32 tie with Midtjylland, along with Rashford.

United had lost the first leg in Denmark 2-1 and, missing several key players through injury, were in danger of going out of Europe.

England forward Wayne Rooney was among those out receiving treatment along with goalkeeper David de Gea, winger Antonio Valencia and defender Chris Smalling.

"The day before the game Van Gaal stuck the starting XI on a board at a team meeting," recalls Riley.

The young player carefully went down the list of familiar names.

Michael Carrick, Daley Blind, Juan Mata, Jesse Lingard, Memphis Depay... Joe Riley!

"I remember thinking: 'Oh my God'. It was a dream come true."

Riley's mum, Derren, and sister, Sophie, were in the 58,609 crowd at Old Trafford to watch him play 79 minutes.

"I had a really good game but I do remember thinking that could be my last for the first team, because the likes of Rojo and Luke Shaw were working their way back from injuries," he says.

While Rashford went on to play several more times that season, including United's FA Cup final win over Crystal Palace at Wembley, Riley did not appear again for the senior side.

He continued to train with the first team even after Van Gaal was sacked and replaced by Jose Mourinho in May 2016, and was named captain of the under-23s.

A damaged hamstring delayed a loan move to Sheffield United and, when the player did eventually arrive at Bramall Lane, the loan was cut short after he dislocated his shoulder.

Riley's 15 years at United ended on 25 May 2018, two years after that magical night against Midtjylland.

While former under-18s team-mate Rashford was preparing to go to the World Cup in Russia with England, Riley joined League One Bradford City on a two-year contract.

Riley's two years with the Bantams included 10 months out with an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. Then there was a long-standing foot issue soon after joining Walsall in 2022, following an injury-free two seasons at League Two Carlisle.

"It took six months to find out what was wrong with my foot and then another three months to recover after surgery," says Riley.

He put those nine months to good use.

Riley started making plans for life after football in case he was forced to retire early because of injury.

"It was getting to the point of wondering if I was ever going to be able to play again because this pain was in my foot and nobody could find it. If you can't find something, how do you fix it?"

Today, he works for a company in Sale, near Manchester, after bringing the curtain down on his full-time playing career after spells in the National League with Fylde and Tamworth.

"I'm loving it," adds Riley about his career in finance protection.

"Moving from full-time football to part-time was something I once feared, like many players do. Instead my job is rewarding, while I joined Warrington Rylands in the summer - a club I thoroughly enjoy being at.

"I've started my exams to become a wealth manager to help with investments and pensions.

"I don't want to play full-time again. Even if an opportunity arose, I'm too far down the road in terms of preparing for life away from football."

Riley's mum can be seen at Warrington Rylands matches supporting her son, just as she did on that cold February Thursday night at Old Trafford all those years ago.

"I will forever be grateful to Manchester United," says Riley, who is engaged to be married to Elizabeth, his partner for the past seven years, next summer in the south of France.

"United turned me into the person I am today - I've got them to thank for that."

And what about Rashford. Is he still in touch with his former academy team-mate?

"I don't have Marcus' number so we don't message. If I bumped into him, I've no doubt it would be just the same as all those years ago when we were growing up together.

"I saw [United boss] Michael Carrick in Portugal this summer and we had a really good chat."

Although he has moved on with his life, Riley does have one regret from his time with United.

Having played a small part in their triumphant 2016 FA Cup campaign, the young United substitute at Shrewsbury wishes he had pressed the club for a winners' medal.

"Had I done so then I probably would have received one," he says.

"I didn't go to Wembley because I wasn't in the squad for the final. At the time I was young and naive, thinking I'd have plenty more opportunities to get a medal.

"In the end I only got to play two first-team games for Manchester United. No-one though will ever be able to take those memories away from me."

title: Why England wing Caluori played on with detached wrist ligament
description: Wing sensation Noah Caluori says he played through the pain of a torn wrist ligament during his break-out season for Saracens and England
fullText:
Teenage wing sensation Noah Caluori has revealed that he spent the majority of his breakthrough season - featuring 18 tries in 13 Prem games and an England debut - playing with a detached ligament in his wrist.

The 19-year-old sustained the injury when he came down heavily on his arm while competing for a high ball in Saracens' defeat by Exeter in December.

After consulting both club and national team coaches, Caluori opted to play through his pain and wait until the summer for an operation to reconnect the ligament.

"It would just hurt," said Caluori. "A lot of movements hurt, I had to modify a lot of my gym plans, catching the high balls hurt.

"I learnt how to manage the pain. That's it, really.

"I came to the conclusion that I'm going to push for this. I'm going to hope that I go on tour [with England], I'm going to try for the best season I can for Saracens, try and help us get to the play-offs.

"You just ride the adrenaline and learn to get on with it."

Caluori posted a picture on social media in July of himself in a hospital bed with a heavily bandaged right wrist.

Explaining now why it felt right to keep playing, he said: "Saracens and England gave me the freedom. If it was too bad and I wasn't able to play, they would have not let me.

"But they gave me the freedom to choose, I chose what I wanted to do, and then you've just got to live with your decision. I was pretty happy that I've done it."

While Saracens fell just short of the Prem play-offs, failing to overhaul Exeter in a final-day shoot-out for a semi-final spot, Caluori succeeded in his other aims.

He finished as the top flight's joint-top try-scorer, made a try-scoring debut for England against Fiji, and then appeared off the bench again in victory over Argentina the following weekend.

Caluori, whose mother Grace is a psychotherapist, regularly lists and revises his goals for the future.

He is determined that his career should not fizzle out, which has happened with some other young prodigies in the past.

"I've had multiple chats with people, and it's just similar things: 'You have the ability to do it, it just matters about your mentality'," said Caluori.

"They've seen loads of players who have done similar to what I've done, then drop off in two or three years because they got complacent.

title: How 'unique' Bellingham is thriving in Mourinho's system
description: Jude Bellingham looks fit and ready to build on his World Cup form as he aims to rediscover his best at Real Madrid under Jose Mourinho.
fullText:
Jude Bellingham has started the new season looking like a player with something to prove.

The 23-year-old's two goals and three assists have helped Real Madrid to an impressive start under new boss Jose Mourinho, with three wins from as many games.

Bellingham's performances, and the freedom he has been given in his new role, has attracted a lot of attention.

Bellingham's last two campaigns were less consistent, with his displays and attacking influence affected not only by a deeper role, but by recurring injuries. He had a long-standing shoulder problem that required surgery in 2025 and a hamstring issue that kept him out for 10 matches in 2026.

Now, however, he appears to be at peak fitness, ready to build on his impressive World Cup form for England and showcase the full extent of his talent.

Since returning this summer to take charge of the club for a second spell, Mourinho has made an important adjustment in reducing the defensive workload that previously meant Bellingham had to cover huge areas of the pitch.

"We've organised the team differently," he said after Real Madrid's 4-0 La Liga win over Malaga.

"Bellingham sometimes defended like a second left-back last season. I told him I do not want to see that anymore. I made a deal with him."

The Portuguese manager has used Bellingham primarily as a number 10 in a 4-2-3-1 system, operating behind French striker Kylian Mbappe and with the freedom to move across the attacking line.

That gives the England midfielder a clearer role. Rather than constantly moving between midfield, defence and attack, he can spend more time in the areas where he is most dangerous.

"For me, this is his position, with his connection with the forwards, he can score goals," added Mourinho.

"He has to play close to the goal. Playing at number six or number eight, we're losing his closeness to the goal. I like this Jude."

It has meant Bellingham can receive the ball between the lines, carry it forward, combine with the forwards and make late runs into the penalty area.

Just as importantly, he is being given greater freedom to decide when to move.

Bellingham has explained the difference himself in an interview with Real Madrid TV.

"I feel more free to decide when to drop back, when to stay up or when to get into the box," he said. "I think this is the best position for me."

Mourinho still expects him to press and recover possession, but the difference is where that work begins.

Instead of dropping deep towards his own penalty area, Bellingham can now use his energy to press opponents higher up the pitch.

When Madrid win the ball, he is already closer to the forwards. That allows him to connect midfield with attack and provide another player who can combine with Mbappe and Vinicius Jr.

It also explains why Mourinho has been keen to stress Madrid's attacking players must work together rather than operate as individuals.

"The team dynamic is about 11, not 2+9," he said.

The midfielder also described working with Mourinho as a "dream", having previously only met the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham manager once before his appointment.

There is clearly an early understanding and respect between the two.

Mourinho has repeatedly spoken about Bellingham's importance to his plans, describing him as a "unique and super important player" with qualities that include physical, mental and tactical.

He also suggested Bellingham should be one of the players in the running for the Ballon d'Or.

"He is a unique kind of player and extremely important for the team," said Mourinho.

"His mental strength, tactical ability, the way he recovers the ball, the way he pressures, the way he plays up front, I am very happy."

For Mourinho, that versatility is part of what makes Bellingham so valuable. He can press, recover possession, score, contribute in the air and drive the team forward.

The Real boss has also pointed to Thomas Tuchel's use of Bellingham at the World Cup as an example of how to get the best out of him.

Bellingham was one of England's standout players, finishing with seven goals and an assist in his eight appearances, and his attacking qualities were allowed to flourish.

That experience also appears to have given the player a confidence boost, particularly as he rejoined Madrid later than most of his team-mates and had less time to prepare for the new campaign.

Although Real's three league wins - scoring 10 goals and conceding two - are only a small sample, and the demands will increase as the season progresses amid Champions League football, the early signs are very positive.

For Bellingham, whose huge strength has always been his ability to affect almost every part of a game, Mourinho's system has given him more control over where that influence is used.

After a difficult couple of seasons following the high standards he set in his first year, the England midfielder is enjoying his football again.

"I'm having a lot of fun, I'm really enjoying my football, and that's why I'm performing well," he told club media.

If he continues in this vein with Mourinho's continued support, it could turn out to be his best season yet.

"I suspect Chelsea will give Arsenal lots of the ball and try to counter-attack quickly," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"The Blues have got some brilliant creativity in Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro, but the fact they are vulnerable at the back could undermine them."

It has been an eventful decade for Foxes fans since they won the Premier League title in 2016 - and not always an enjoyable one.

Since then, they have seen their side reach the Champions League quarter-finals, lift the FA Cup and Community Shield, win promotion from the Championship and suffer three relegations, including last season when they went down to League One.

"Promotion!" said Serge. "It has to be. I love the play-offs, so a win at Wembley would do me."

A new-look Leicester side took their first step towards bouncing back when they picked up their opening win of the season against Plymouth on Tuesday, but Serge added Russell Martin's youthful side will need time to fully find their feet in the third tier.

"I hope they get it," he said. "Patience is so important in football, and young teams should play with no fear."

My daughter's old maths teacher, Mr Fields, is an Ipswich fan and he is very excited about how ambitious the club has been since getting promoted. I think all their supporters must be the same.

Ipswich have spent almost £200m on a stack of new signings to try to stay in the Premier League and, watching them, it is clear they are not just planning to park the bus.

They will be confident for this game after beating Sunderland at home on the opening weekend and I am expecting them to have a real go at Liverpool too.

It will be interesting to see if new signing Bradley Barcola starts for the Reds, who seem to have a lot of attacking players who like to play off the left.

Boss Andoni Iraola has plenty of attacking options, but I still have concerns about them defensively, while his players adjust to his front-foot pressing style.

I am sure he will get it right eventually, but at the moment they are leaking goals and creaking at the back.

My gut feeling is Ipswich will score, but Liverpool will still edge the win after two successive 2-2 draws. If their attack clicks, it will be hard to keep them out.

Newcastle have started the season superbly with four points, and it feels like they have changed the mood at St James' Park after a difficult summer.

There's no doom and gloom about the place despite them losing several key players and, after predicting they would lose their first two games, I feel differently about their prospects now.

Things can change very quickly of course and a home defeat by Bournemouth would see a lot of that optimism disappear. But, so far, I've been really impressed by Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa looks like he has got his confidence back.

I like the way new manager Matthias Jaissle has set them up to hit teams on the counter-attack, and Nico Gonzalez looks like a sensible signing too.

I called Newcastle 'a development club' before their first game, because of the type of players they have bought and sold this summer, but while their midfield is quite youthful, they have now got Nico in there to give them a bit of extra clout.

This is still a tricky game to call, however.

Bournemouth haven't won yet, but only because they have let leads slip away late on, first against Manchester City and then at home to Everton.

Cherries boss Marco Rose is another manager who likes to play on the front foot and they are certainly capable of getting something here, even though I have gone for a home win.

I was spot on with my predictions for both of these teams last week, but I still don't feel very confident about calling the outcome of this game.

Brentford are a brilliant counter-attacking side who seem especially strong at home.

I was erring towards backing the Bees to win, like they did in this fixture last season, but then had second thoughts.

I backed the Black Cats to win their first two matches (see the table based on Sutton's predictions at the bottom of the page) because they are a well-organised team, with plenty of physicality and also a threat up top.

My concern for them is what happens when European football starts, but that hasn't happened yet. I don't see them losing this.

I am not really sure what to make of Brighton yet. They smashed Aston Villa on the opening weekend but then lost to Chelsea despite dominating possession in what was a really strange game.

Leeds can be quite cagey on the road under Daniel Farke, but they are very good at what they do, and they will be a threat on the break.

I am still going with Brighton to win because they are playing with freedom at the moment, but I don't see them keeping a clean sheet and this is going to be close.

Neither of these teams have got a point so far, as I predicted.

On top of his side's poor start to the season, one of the problems for Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage will be dealing with Ismaila Sarr after he did not get a move to Liverpool before the transfer window shut.

My worry for Fulham is they have become a Real Madrid feeder team, and their boss Alvaro Arbeloa has already got issues with his squad.

He stuck the boot into his players after their defeat by Sunderland, questioning their mentality.

A first win would be massive for both new managers, but I don't think either of them will get it here.

This is a tale of two Citys - one of whom has made the best of starts to the season, while the other has had the worst.

Manchester City wiped the floor with Crystal Palace last week but it was their comeback to beat Bournemouth at the Etihad which felt bigger, because it was the beginning of a new era under Enzo Maresca.

In contrast, Coventry City have had a terrible time. Not their 3-0 opening defeat at Arsenal, because they can forget about that, but they must feel so deflated after losing 1-0 at home to another promoted side in Hull last time out.

This game is more like the Arsenal one, in that no-one is expecting Coventry to get anything, but the upshot is they are likely to be left without a point or even a goal after their first three games.

There were some doubts about Manchester City after the way they lost the Community Shield against Arsenal, but they look a different proposition already.

Maresca has made more signings in the past few days, including Enzo Fernandez from his old club Chelsea for £125m. I've heard people question whether Fernandez is worth the big money that City paid, but Maresca knows him well and I see him as a great addition to their midfield.

I said before the Bournemouth game I didn't think they could win the title without Rodri, but they have rebuilt their midfield now with Fernandez and Ayyoub Bouaddi joining Elliot Anderson as new signings, and they have got real strength in there now.

I like Erling Haaland's new haircut too. It suits him far more than a ponytail. He looks a bit rougher and tougher and I don't think Coventry will keep him out.

Nottingham Forest are waiting for their first win under Oliver Glasner but I felt they were unlucky to lose against Leeds and also to only draw at Liverpool.

I have been very disappointed with Roberto de Zerbi's Tottenham so far, however, and not just because of their poor results.

When he came in at Brighton, De Zerbi built an amazing team in a short space of time and they were great to watch even if they made a few mistakes along the way.

In contrast, we still don't know what his Spurs team are about, even though they have spent an absolute fortune on players.

I think that's on De Zerbi because, although new players take time to gel, his side have put in two really insipid performances so far.

He has put that down to the team not being fully fit and blamed their pre-season schedule, but they should still be doing much better than they are - with no points and no goals so far.

Other clubs, with new managers as well as lots of new players, look much more organised so it is not an excuse.

Still, Spurs have surely got to improve soon, which is why I have got them down to pick up a first point here.

Hull will be on such a high after winning their first two games, and that makes this game even harder to predict.

The Tigers are really well organised and are not bothered about how much possession they have, they are just bothered about being effective when they do get the ball.

They defend the box brilliantly but there will still be a few weeks this season where teams run all over them because of the way they are set up.

Aston Villa won't necessarily do that, but I still think they will come out on top despite their poor start to the new campaign.

Ollie Watkins is a big loss but they have got Nicolas Jackson in to lead their line, who I think is a good signing.

It took Villa six games to register their first league win last season, but they won't have to wait as long this time.

Everton ended up keeping hold of young midfielder Harrison Armstrong but they made a mess of their attempts to sign another striker before the transfer window closed.

I know Thierno Barry comes in for criticism and his finishing is erratic, but at least they still have him to lead their line.

He scores some brilliant goals too, as does Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, so I don't think it will be all doom and gloom for Everton fans this season, despite their frustration at the moment.

As for Manchester United, well I know some of their supporters think I am down on them all the time.

So, I'd like to point out I backed them to win their first two games of the season and they are joint top of the table (below) based on my predictions.

This time, I'm going for a draw, but that would still be a decent result for Michael Carrick's side.

Arsenal were a bit clunky last time out against Aston Villa, while I love what Xabi Alonso is doing at Chelsea.

He doesn't care about possession, and that's not how Chelsea try to get results.

It's strange because I had a look at how his Bayer Leverkusen side lined up when they won the Bundesliga, and they were pretty dominant possession-wise.

So, it is quite alarming when you look at the two league games Chelsea have played and see how much of the ball they haven't had. Against Fulham they only had 38% possession and then against Brighton it was down to 25%.

I don't know whether that is by design or by just not having the players to dominate. They are still free-scoring, but they are conceding loads of goals too.

Whatever the reason, I don't see it changing here. Arsenal are so powerful and the only question mark around them is if they are a forward or two short.

Even so, you would not exactly say they have a real weakness anywhere. The beauty of Mikel Arteta's side is they can play in different ways.

They demolished Manchester City in the Community Shield with some pure football, and played some nice stuff against Coventry too, but then they were able to grind out a win at Aston Villa as well.

Ultimately, whether they are free-flowing or not, their organisation should see them through this game too.

Chris picked up his first win of the season after getting seven correct results - including three exact scores - from the 10 matches in week two.

After a slow start, five of his correct results - and two of his exact scores - came in the five games on Sunday and Monday.

That gave him a total of 160 points, enough to hold off a strong challenge from the BBC readers and AI.

The collective efforts of the readers helped them get six correct results, with two exact scores, for 120 points.

Like Chris, AI managed seven correct results, but with only one exact score, leaving it on 100 points.

Chris' guest, Royal Blood drummer Ben Thatcher, did not fare so well. He got four correct results with no exact scores, and ended up with 40 points.

"It's not how you start the weekend, it's how you finish it," Sutton said. "I am burying AI at the moment, which is a lovely feeling."

Everyone was right about three of the fixtures - Manchester City's win at Crystal Palace, Manchester United's victory over Ipswich and Arsenal's success at Aston Villa.

There were only two fixtures where none of our predictors picked the right outcome - Liverpool's draw with Nottingham Forest and Hull's win at Coventry.

From almost 37,000 predictions for the latter, only around 5,000 (15%) of you backed the Tigers to take the three points, and fewer than 1,500 (4%) went for them to win by a 1-0 scoreline.

title: 100 influencers invited to US Open spark debate on 'tennis etiquette'
description: The behaviour of influencers and content creators has become a major talking point at this year's US Open amid incidents of matches being disrupted.
fullText:
Lights. Camera. Quiet please...

When it comes to etiquette in tennis, there are a fair few unwritten rules.

Apologising after winning a point from a net cord. Honesty around line calls, double bounces and double-hits. Post-match handshakes.

As for the spectators, it is common courtesy not to disturb the players during points.

Around 100 influencers and content creators have been granted accreditation for the tournament in New York - double the amount from last year.

Their presence has led to debate over how to balance bringing tennis to a new, different audience while respecting the game's etiquette.

"I definitely think it's cool to have a new demographic and I definitely think it helps grow the sport," world number four Coco Gauff said.

"But if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans.

"I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport. That's all."

During two-time champion Naomi Osaka's first-round match on Arthur Ashe Stadium, one group held a photo shoot in their hospitality suite while play was going on.

The group turned on a portable ring light while Osaka was serving, leading to a reprimand from the umpire.

When Osaka returned on Thursday, the umpire had to remind the crowd several times to be quiet.

"Today the umpire told everyone to be quiet more than I've ever heard an umpire tell a crowd to be quiet," Osaka said.

"I tell people I normally just focus on the match and the court, but there was a moment where there was people shouting and you could hear it quite clearly.

"I think it bothered my opponent, too."

In one video, which has gone viral, a group can be seen speaking loudly as they film themselves during Osaka's first-round match on Tuesday, which led to the chair umpire calling for them to stop.

"I think obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport," Osaka said.

"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette.

"It could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like my first-round match.

"Overall, I think there are huge positives. You want people to continue to grow the sport.

"I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."

No Britons left in US Open singles as Dart & Jones lose

Arthur Ashe is the biggest tennis stadium in the world, and matches are often accompanied by a buzz of noise from conversations around the arena.

Some players love it. Some do not.

Men's seventh seed Daniil Medvedev, who has had a tricky relationship with the New York crowds in the past, believes whatever brings more eyes to tennis can only be a good thing.

"I think the more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is," the Russian said.

"The more the sport grows, the better it is. I trust USTA [tournament organisers the United States Tennis Association] with what they are doing.

"I think [there is] a lot more upside than downside, so go for it."

American 11th seed Frances Tiafoe praised the diversity of the crowd in New York.

"I think the Open is great because you get all types of people that want to come and watch tennis," he said.

"All different walks of life, different types of people, different type of occupations. Personally, I love that.

"I have no problem with anybody doing anything, coming to watch the tennis."

American world number three Jessica Pegula, however, said some of the behaviour had been "disrespectful".

"I can appreciate the influencers coming and showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said.

"But I do think that it's tough when you see videos when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.

"People are down there trying to perform. It's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful.

"I think it's become a little too much this year.

"I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."

The US Open introduced a policy of free fan movement in 2024, meaning fans no longer have to wait to take their seats during changeovers.

A year later, the tournament was expanded to 15 days. The week before the singles draw is now marketed as a 'Fan Week', showcasing the revamped mixed doubles competition and exhibition matches between players past and present.

It is all part of what tournament chief executive Craig Tiley hopes will become "the tennis Disneyland".

Tiley, asked about influencers being accredited in a pre-tournament news conference, said: "We need to find ways of reaching new audiences, reaching people in a way that they connect with media today.

"The creation of the creator credential has been a key part of that because it's enabled us to talk to people in a way that they're listening. That's been a big focus."

Since the incident in Osaka's first match, there has been increased messaging on screens around the ground reminding people to "refrain from any activity that could disrupt the game, including noise levels, flash photography and ring lights".

The USTA said in a statement it "is always striving to grow tennis in this country and bring new audiences into the sport".

"We want all of our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend, but we also need to ensure they do not interfere with the action and competition on the court," it added.

"We are continually looking for ways to ensure fans in the stands know what is permitted and what is prohibited."

title: Ukrainian quits college team over Russian signing
description: Ukrainian Kate Koval says she left Louisiana State University's basketball program because of the team's decision to sign a Russian player.
fullText:
Ukrainian Kate Koval says she left Louisiana State University's basketball program because of the team's decision to sign a Russian player.

Following the arrival of Anna Minaeva, it was announced that 20-year-old Koval had departed for "personal reasons" after one season.

Koval said Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine was why she stepped away.

"My father serves in the Ukrainian military and takes tremendous pride in defending his country against Russian aggression," she wrote on Instagram.

"For me, this war is not distant or abstract. People close to me have been killed and wounded in Russian attacks, and places where I grew up and first began playing basketball have been destroyed by missile strikes.

"The timing of this situation and the deep personal effect it has had on me, my family and those we care about who continue to live through and fight this war ultimately made me question whether LSU remained the right place for me.

"This decision has not been easy. While I understand and respect that roster decisions are a part of college basketball, I have to remain true to myself, my values and my country."

Koval, who was expected to be LSU's starting centre this year, has two years of collegiate eligibility remaining.

The transfer portal has closed, but she said she hopes the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) "recognises the circumstances surrounding my situation and understands the seriousness and deep nature of this matter" and allows her to join a different university for the upcoming season.

Koval said: "I felt I had found a home at LSU, and I am incredibly grateful for my team-mates who became family, as well as my coaches, staff, professors and the entire LSU community.

"I will always cherish the relationships, experiences, and memories I made there."

title: Trio of Iowa football legends named to USA TODAY's all-2000s team
description: A trio of Iowa football legends were named to USA TODAY Sports' all-2000s team.
fullText:
The Iowa football program has seen many great players don the black and gold over the past 25 years.

The Kirk Ferentz era has brought a ton of success on and off the field for the Hawkeyes. Great players have led to wins and the most prosperous, sustained period of Iowa football ever. Even among all the greats, there are certain guys that stand out among the pack.

USA TODAY Sports identified a trio of Hawks from the Ferentz era who differentiated themselves from the rest. Writers Paul Myerberg, Eddie Timanus and Craig Meyer put together their All-2000's college football teams. The two teams consist of the best college football players from the dawn of the century until right now. Mixed in among the two teams were three Iowa football legends.

Iowa had one representative on the All-2000's first team: punter Tory Taylor. The writers had the following to say about the fan-favorite Aussie:

"Perhaps no program's fans appreciate their punter more than Iowa's, and few did it better than Taylor. The 2023 Ray Guy Award winner helped the Hawkeyes to a 10-3 record as a senior despite the team averaging just 16.6 points a game. Taylor averaged 46.3 yards per punt over his career and led the Bowl Subdivision in kicks downed inside the 20 three years in a row."

Two more Hawkeyes appeared on the All-2000's second team: tight end Dallas Clark and kicker Nate Kaeding. Clark was a mainstay on Iowa's offense for both the 2001 and 2002 seasons. Across those two years, he compiled 81 career receptions for 1,281 yards and eight touchdowns. He was named an All-American in 2002 and went on to be a first-round pick in the 2003 NFL Draft.

Kaeding is Iowa's career scoring leader with 373 points. The 2002 recipient of the Lou Groza Award, Kaeding was also a consensus All-American following his standout 2003 season. Kaeding made 67 field goals in his Hawkeye career and booted through 22 consecutive kicks at one point spanning the 2001 and 2002 seasons.
