fullText:
The FIBA World Cup tips off on Friday with a 16-team field. More than 50 WNBA players, who are on a two-week break from the league, will take part in the competition as the United States seeks its fifth consecutive title, and 15 other federations attempt to dethrone the champs.

Here's what to know as play begins:

It's hard to overstate the Americans' dominance in international competition. Since the creation of the WNBA, Team USA is undefeated in the Olympics — only three wins have come by single digits since 1996 — and it has lost only once in the world championships, which led to a third-place finish in 2006. The Americans have cleaned up at the four world championships since, with double-figure victories in every game but one during that stretch.

Even without A'ja Wilson on this year's roster, Team USA still has the best individual player in the tournament (whether you consider that to be Breanna Stewart, Caitlin Clark, Napheesa Collier or someone else, it's an American) and the best collection of talent. It would be a considerable upset for the Americans to be beaten. Four of Team USA's closest contests during the last 20 years, including the one loss, came to Russia, but that program has fallen off. Since its decline, no true basketball rival has emerged for the United States.

USA Basketball heavily values international tournaments, from the youth level onward. It's why the WNBA, which is the world's premier basketball league, would take a break right before the postseason to accommodate the World Cup and why the best players in this league are eschewing a break of their own to compete. Success on the global stage matters.

For all of the skill Team USA brings to the table, it lost a lot of experience when Wilson (Las Vegas Aces) and Kelsey Plum (Phoenix Mercury) opted out of the tournament due to injuries. The pair have each competed in two Olympics and two World Cups, and Wilson has been the Americans' leading scorer at the last three major international competitions.

Without that duo, Team USA is left with three players with World Cup experience; Breanna Stewart is suiting up for the fourth time, while Chelsea Gray and Kahleah Copper both were on the 2022 roster. Only five players have represented the U.S. in five-on-five at a senior tournament (Rhyne Howard played 3×3 at the last Olympics). The team is so green that four players haven't even appeared in a WNBA playoff game.

Even the coaching staff is a little inexperienced at the international level. Duke coach Kara Lawson has come up through USA Basketball. She coached the inaugural 3×3 team in Tokyo, was an assistant during the last cycle under Cheryl Reeve and won the AmeriCup in 2025 with a roster of college players. But this is the first rodeo for the assistants: Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White, Phoenix coach Nate Tibbetts and Golden State Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase. It will be interesting to see how these coaches respond to game pressure; none has been the head coach of a WNBA or NCAA champion.

During the qualifying tournament, the U.S. tended to start its veterans even though the minutes were relatively evenly distributed. Although Clark started one game, she played enough to earn MVP of the event. Lawson is expected to pick a more experienced starting five — something that includes Stewart, Gray and Copper plus one more guard and a center.

This is an opportunity for Stewart to assert herself as a leader. She has more international experience than just about all of her teammates combined, and she was the MVP of this tournament in 2018. Stewart and Wilson have been the co-stewards of this era of USA Basketball, but the New York Liberty superstar is the only one in Berlin.

Australia has been the most consistently competitive team in international competitions over the past two decades, and it finished third in the 2022 World Cup and the 2024 Olympics. The Opals have eight WNBA players, six of whom are currently meaningful rotation players: Alanna Smith (Dallas Wings), Rebecca Allen (Liberty), Ezi Magbegor (Seattle Storm), Jade Melbourne (Storm), Isobel Borlase (Atlanta Dream) and Stephanie Talbot (Aces). What Australia is missing is a singular offensive engine; it's unclear how the Opals can manufacture quality offense in the half court, even if their defensive upside is as good as anyone in the tournament.

Belgium has been the class of the European teams, winners of the last two EuroBasket competitions. Forward Emma Meesseman, the 2019 WNBA Finals MVP who has played only two full WNBA seasons since, always brings it for her national team. Her skill in the post as a passing hub and a scorer is near-unmatched, and she is flanked by two dynamic guards in Julie Allemand (Toronto Tempo) and Julie Vanloo, who are willing creators and attackers.

Mike Thibault is a veteran coach (the second-winningest in WNBA history) who spent time with Meesseman on the Washington Mystics and has been an assistant at the Olympics. The Belgians have something of an it factor, too — they won the 2025 European championship in regulation despite trailing Spain by 12 with 2:42 to play.

One caveat to Belgium's 2025 victory was that the French essentially punted on the tournament. Gabby Williams, Marine Johannès and Dominique Malonga all stayed with their WNBA teams instead of reporting. The last time France had a full roster was at the Paris Olympics 2024, when the home team was one foot away from taking Team USA to overtime in the gold-medal game.

France has an impressive collection of perimeter talent. Among Williams (Valkyries), Carla Leite (Portland Fire) and Pauline Astier (Liberty), several guards can blow by their initial defender and break down a defense. Leite is one week removed from giving Angel Reese and Howard fits in Atlanta, while Astier has tormented the Fever duo of Clark and Aliyah Boston. This is a guard group that will demand that the U.S. defend on a string, which is a tricky thing for a 12-player roster that hasn't ever played together. They are mostly good defenders, too. A backcourt of Williams and Leïla Lacan can cause discomfort for even the American stars.

The French have great spacing throughout their lineup. Johannès and Janelle Salaün (Valkyries) are some of the most willing shooters in the world, and their unorthodox shot releases keep good defense from deterring them. Salaün relishes a contest on her 3-pointer and shoots better with a defender in her face.

France isn't as imposing in the frontcourt, though Salaün and Malonga are a devastating starting combo with the former's shooting and the latter's rim-running. Malonga is also one of the better paint protectors in the entire tournament. Team USA will need to have success from beyond the arc to break France's defense.

Nigeria has quietly given Team USA trouble in recent competitions. It lost by nine to the Americans in the 2020 Olympics group stage and by 14 in the quarterfinals of the 2024 Olympics. Rena Wakama, a current Unrivaled head coach and Chicago Sky assistant, has done a fantastic job establishing a team culture for Nigeria. The group moves the ball well, plays hard and uses its athleticism effectively.

China is the biggest team in the tournament, though it took a sizable hit when 6-foot-7 Li Yueru (Wings) was ruled out due to passport issues. Nevertheless, in addition to 6-11 Han Xu (Liberty), keep an eye on 7-3 Zhang Ziyu. The 19-year-old center is eligible for the 2027 WNBA Draft and could improve her stock with a strong showing in Berlin. Unfortunately, the less said about China's guards, the better; their main job is to get the ball past half court without turning it over and then feed the bigs.

Spain has the most active WNBA players (five) among remaining teams, including Storm rookie Awa Fam. An especially intriguing player to watch is Iyana Martín, the Fire's first-round pick, who will be coming stateside next season. Martín has a phenomenal track record at junior competitions, including winning MVP of the 2023 U-19 World Cup when Spain lost in the finals' overtime to the U.S. That group is all grown up, and this is now Martín's first foray at the senior level, where she has just the right amount of flair and playmaking verve to complement the rock-solid production of Megan DiLeo (Fire) in the paint.

Every Team USA game will be on TNT or truTV, and the entire tournament can be streamed on HBO Max.

title: Carragher: Chiesa ‘never going to kick a ball’ after Liverpool Champions League omission
description: Liverpool legend Jamie Carragher says Federico Chiesa is ‘never going to kick a ball’ with the Reds this season after the Italian winger was omitted from their Champions League squad list.Liverpoo...
fullText:
Liverpool legend Jamie Carragher says Federico Chiesa is 'never going to kick a ball' with the Reds this season after the Italian winger was omitted from their Champions League squad list.

Liverpool have left Chiesa out of their Champions League squad list for the first part of the 2026-27 season.

NEWCASTLE UPON TYNE, ENGLAND – AUGUST 25: Federico Chiesa of Liverpool during the Premier League match between Newcastle United and Liverpool at St James' Park on August 25, 2025 in Newcastle upon Tyne, England. (Photo by George Wood/Getty Images)

Chiesa has scored five goals in 50 appearances across all competitions with Liverpool since 2024 and is currently out of action due to a muscle problem.

"Liverpool have got two players in the squad who are never going to play," Carragher said, speaking on the Overlap, via Goal.com.

"And there are all these quotas; you can only have 17 players and all that. They have got Chiesa and Endo. It's like they are never going to kick a ball."

Liverpool's Federico Chiesa reacts during the UEFA Champions League soccer match between AC Milan and Liverpool FC at Giuseppe Meazza stadium in Milan, 17 September 2024. EPA-EFE/MATTEO BAZZI

While Chiesa has been left out of Liverpool's Champions League squad, another Italy international, Giovanni Leoni, features in the list. The promising centre-back is recovering from a cruciate ligament injury, and Andoni Iraola has said that he's expected to return to team training during the international break between the end of September and the start of October.

LIVERPOOL, ENGLAND – SEPTEMBER 23: Giovanni Leoni of Liverpool receives medical treatment to an injury before being substituted off during the Carabao Cup Third Round match between Liverpool and Southampton at Anfield on September 23, 2025 in Liverpool, England. (Photo by Stu Forster/Getty Images)

title: Report: Sunderland star on the verge of shock exit
description: Chemsdine Talbi transfer talks leave Sunderland facing fresh Europa League questionsSunderland have left the door open to a late Chemsdine Talbi exit after omitting the winger from their Europa League...
fullText:
Sunderland have left the door open to a late Chemsdine Talbi exit after omitting the winger from their Europa League squad, a decision that looks closely tied to ongoing transfer discussions. As first reported by talkSPORT, the 21-year-old is in talks with Al-Ittihad, while Galatasaray and Fenerbahce are also showing interest before their respective windows close.

It is a development that carries weight. Talbi only joined Sunderland from Club Brugges for £18 million last summer and, despite flashes of promise, his first year on Wearside brought an uneven role. He was used only sporadically and was among the substitutes in the 1-0 win over Fulham last weekend. Now, with the Premier League window shut but Saudi Arabia and Turkey still active, Sunderland are dealing with a situation that remains live.

The Europa League squad list offered the clearest indication yet that Talbi's future is under discussion. Sunderland named Robin Roefs and Simon Moore as goalkeepers, with defenders Omar Alderete, Dan Ballard, Kevin Danso, Trai Hume, Reinildo, Dayann Méthalie, Thomas Meunier, Nordi Mukiele and Luke O'Nien included. Midfielders Jules Ahoka, Habib Diarra, Enzo Le Fee, Chris Rigg, Noah Sadiki and Granit Xhaka also made the cut, alongside forwards Nilson Angulo, Brian Brobbey, Malick Fofana, Wilson Isidor and Romaine Mundle.

Talbi cannot be added via List B because, while he is age-eligible, he has not been at the club for the required two-year period. In practical terms, that leaves him outside Sunderland's immediate European plans and naturally intensifies scrutiny around a potential sale or loan.

Regis Le Bris addressed the matter directly and his remarks were measured, while also confirming the possibility of movement. The Sunderland head coach said, "A move remains possible so it's important to respect both parties. We'll see." He added, "He's still a good player, huge potential but after that you still have a window to decide if it's the right pathway here."

Perhaps most revealing was the final line from Le Bris, "I believe he can succeed here, but after that it's a question of mutual confidence and you have to respect the player's choice." That wording suggests Sunderland are not actively forcing the player out, but they are realistic about the market and the player's own thinking.

Talbi scored four times in 28 Premier League appearances last season and later earned selection in Morocco's 26-man World Cup squad for North America. Those details explain why clubs remain interested, even if Sunderland have yet to see the best of him consistently. From the club's point of view, the decision now looks like a balancing act between protecting squad harmony, managing an unsettled player and safeguarding value on a recent £18 million investment.

With Al-Ittihad, Galatasaray and Fenerbahce all in the frame, this feels like a situation to watch closely in the final days of those open markets. Sunderland may still hope Talbi stays and develops, but leaving him out of the Europa League squad has made this one of the club's most significant late-window stories.

From an unhappy Sunderland supporter's perspective, this is exactly the sort of story that sets alarm bells ringing. You spend £18 million on a young winger, talk up his upside, give it a year, then suddenly he is out of the Europa League squad while clubs in Saudi Arabia and Turkey circle. It all feels too familiar, too untidy, and too easy for Sunderland to present as a calm, mutual situation when supporters are left wondering why another talented player seems halfway out the door.

Le Bris saying, "A move remains possible so it's important to respect both parties. We'll see," is fair enough in public, but fans will hear that and think the club are braced for him to go. The line, "it's a question of mutual confidence and you have to respect the player's choice," may be honest, yet it also raises a bigger concern. Why has that confidence dropped so quickly after one season?

Talbi may not have torn the league apart, but four goals in 28 Premier League games at his age is hardly a reason to give up. If anything, Sunderland should be finding ways to bring him on, especially after qualifying for Europe. Leaving him out makes the situation look strategic, perhaps even final, and that is frustrating for supporters who want ambition backed up by patience.

If he goes now, fans will rightly ask what the plan was. Buy for £18 million, develop for a year, then move on before he can contribute in Europe? That is not the sort of squad building that inspires confidence. Sunderland need stability, conviction and stronger messaging than this.

title: Report: Liverpool rejected deadline day offer for forward
description: Liverpool reject Keyrol Figueroa bid as Port Vale loan offers clearer route to senior footballLiverpool turned down a seven-figure offer for Keyrol Figueroa before sanctioning his deadline day loan to...
fullText:
Liverpool turned down a seven-figure offer for Keyrol Figueroa before sanctioning his deadline day loan to Port Vale, according to Liverpool.com, in a move that says plenty about how the club currently view the young striker.

Transfer deadline day was relatively calm at Anfield, but this was one of the more interesting developments beneath the surface. Figueroa, a highly regarded 20-year-old forward, had attracted interest from a number of markets, with Liverpool.com reporting that approaches arrived from Ligue 2 in France, Major League Soccer and Portugal. One unnamed club went further and placed a seven-figure proposal on the table for a permanent transfer, only for Liverpool to reject it.

That stance is significant. Liverpool have clearly decided that Figueroa remains an asset worth protecting, even if he is not yet in a position to force his way into Andoni Iraola's first-team plans. The head coach approved a temporary move instead, with the club choosing Port Vale as the destination for a player in need of regular senior minutes.

The immediate picture at Anfield helps explain the decision. Figueroa was involved during pre-season and wanted to make his case ahead of the new Premier League campaign, but the pathway looked crowded. He has found himself behind Jayden Danns and Will Wright in the attacking queue, while Josh Sonni-Lambie has also stepped up into the under-21s environment.

Even so, Liverpool's refusal to cash in suggests they believe there is still substantial upside. The report states that "they feel the frontman has a big future ahead of him and a loan was preferred rather than allowing the player to move on a permanent switch." That is a notable message for a player who is yet to make his professional debut for Liverpool's senior side.

His academy return offers encouragement. Across 26 Premier League 2 appearances, Figueroa scored 12 goals, enough to maintain interest internally and externally. He was also named in the senior matchday squad for the Carabao Cup fourth-round tie against Crystal Palace last October, another indicator that his progress has been monitored closely.

For now, Port Vale presents the opportunity Liverpool feel he needs. After Vale's relegation last term, there should be scope for Figueroa to play meaningful football in a demanding environment, and that is often where a young striker's next stage of development is best judged.

Manager Jon Brady's assessment made clear why the League Two club were keen. "Keyrol comes from an outstanding football environment at Liverpool and has a really exciting attacking profile," Brady said. "He's quick, direct and dynamic, with a real desire to threaten defenders and play on the front foot."

Brady added, "He has the strength and technical ability to receive the ball under pressure and link play, while also having the pace and athleticism to run in behind, attack space and cause problems with his movement."

That profile fits a forward capable of stretching games, and Brady also highlighted another quality that stands out: "There's an unpredictability to him in attacking areas which I feel is something we need and will add another dimension to our team."

He continued, "His goalscoring record at PL2 level speaks for itself, particularly in terms of his goals-per-game return, but he's still a young player with plenty of development ahead of him. We're really excited to work with Keyrol, help him continue that development and give him the freedom to express the qualities he has."

Figueroa's story already carries an international dimension. He has represented Honduras at senior level, making his first appearance in a 2-0 defeat to Argentina in June after switching allegiance from the USA, whom he had represented at youth level.

Now comes a pivotal campaign. Liverpool's decision to reject a permanent offer and prioritise a loan shows confidence, but it also places responsibility on the player. If he thrives at Port Vale, scores goals and proves he can handle the physical and tactical demands of senior football, he will return with a stronger case to be reconsidered in Iraola's wider plans next summer.

From a Liverpool supporter's perspective, this feels like the right call. A seven-figure offer sounds tempting for a player without a senior appearance, but the club clearly believe Keyrol Figueroa could be worth far more, either on the pitch or in the market, if he develops properly over the next 12 months.

There is also something reassuring in the fact that Liverpool did not simply take the money and move on. Too often, young forwards can get lost between academy football and the first team, especially when competition is fierce. By choosing a loan, the club are effectively saying they still want to learn more about him in a proper men's football environment.

Port Vale looks like a smart landing spot. He should get the sort of rough-edged experience that under-21 football cannot always provide, and if Jon Brady uses him consistently, Liverpool will get a much clearer read on whether Figueroa can genuinely push on.

The quotes about him being "quick, direct and dynamic" and offering "unpredictability" are the sort of descriptions that immediately catch the eye. Supporters always respond to attackers who can make something happen. If he starts scoring early, people will take notice fast.

For now, patience is key. Figueroa does not need hype, he needs games, goals and rhythm. Liverpool rejecting a permanent bid may yet prove to be a very smart piece of business.

title: 73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
description: Harry Kane was the highest goalscorer in Europe last season, yet he plays like a midfielder. We ask him to break down his game.
fullText:
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

title: Jackson Wolf throws six hitless innings, Lakeland launches three homers

fullText:
Jackson Wolf delivered six hitless innings, and Toledo reclaimed the lead in the eighth to earn its third consecutive win over Indianapolis. Four Mud Hens pitchers combined to allow just one hit while striking out 12.

Wolf's only two blemishes were a leadoff walk in the second and a hit batter in the fifth. The latter looked like it might have caught the knob of Tyler Callihan's bat, but there's no replay to review that in the minors.

Wolf filled up the strike zone over six innings, throwing 54 strikes on 72 pitches. He struck out five with his sweeper and eight overall, generating 13 whiffs on 41 swings. Wolf's command of his secondary pitches was a thing of beauty today. His sweeper was lethal in two-strike counts and averaged 11 inches of horizontal break.

"it's a swing and a miss"
Another DAY on the Bump for Wolfie pic.twitter.com/jH0SPDFjKP

The no-hit line is a bit deceptive. Indianapolis put 10 balls in play against Wolf, including six hard hits, but some good defense from Michael Siani in center field, among others, bailed him out a few times.

Wolf's only problem was that the offense provided hardly any run support. The Mud Hens squandered an early opportunity in the second, when Siani struck out with the bases loaded. James Outman grounded into Toledo's second double play of the game earlier in the inning.

Andrew Navigato doubled with one out in the fifth and advanced to third on a groundout, but the Hens stranded him there. They finally broke the scoreless tie in the sixth. Corey Julks doubled with one out, and Jung drove him home with a single to center.

The Holy Sheetz Play of the Game goes to the first RBI of the night !! @sheetz pic.twitter.com/FiOX7A6HKn

Hayden Minton preserved the lead and extended the combined no-hit bid in the seventh, working around a leadoff walk. Ty Madden took over in the eighth and struck out the first batter he faced before Nick Cimillo gave the Indians their first hit of the day, a game-tying solo homer to center.

The Mud Hens answered in the bottom half. Jung collected his third base knock of the game, and Outman walked before Seby Zavala bunted both runners into scoring position. Indianapolis intentionally walked Chris Meyers to load the bases, and Navigato brought Jung home with a force out.

Madden returned for the ninth but walked Enmanuel Valdez with one out. Tanner Rainey took over and retired the final two batters, securing the victory and Rainey's third save.

Wetwiska got through the third 1-2-3, but he gave up a solo shot and two singles while recording only one out in the fourth. Zack Lee took over and stranded both runners, preserving a 3-2 lead.

fullText:
As one card recently sold for £12m, opportunistic thefts have surged – envelopes are being opened en route, costing small businesses thousands

Pokémon’s success over the last 30 years has seen it grow from a much-loved Game Boy classic, to a world-dominating brand with TV shows, spin-off games, toys and even a theme park. The trading card game is a huge part of that, with more than 85bn cards printed over its lifetime, and the appetite for them shows no signs of slowing down. Packs get snapped up after release so quickly it’s now almost impossible to find them in shops, and a booming resale market is driving the hobby into murky waters.

One card recently sold for an eye-watering £12m, and an increasing number of people have gotten into the collecting business on the hunt for huge profits, leading to a rise in thefts targeting card shops. More recently though, some small businesses have reported that their sales have been hit by thieves targeting envelopes within Royal Mail, leading to thousands in lost revenue.

Ben Thyer, owner of Bath TCG – a card specialist store in the Bath area, is one of those affected. “We always get the odd parcel going missing, but because it was sporadic, we put that down to unfortunate incidents,” Thyer tells the Guardian. “Then [in late July], we had a message [from a customer] with pictures of a cut-open envelope, and the cards were missing. Then there was a second, and then a third, and then there were seven – all of them from the same batch shipped on the same day. We asked for images from each person, and every envelope had been Sellotaped … we don’t use Sellotape because we have brand new envelopes, and we use our own labels over the seals. It’s clear someone had done it deliberately.”

The images, seen by the Guardian, show that the mailed envelopes were tampered with in the exact same way. Thyer considers it clear that this was a targeted theft rather than a coincidence. Fortunately, those particular cards weren’t of high value, but he has since had to close down online card sales, considering the risk of theft and damaged reputation to his business to be too high. By stopping those sales he has now lost out on £4,000-6,000 of potential revenue, a huge amount for a small business.

Bath TCG is not the only card sales business to be affected, and the issue is not just affecting Pokémon cards. Daniel Stack, director of Mana Rock Games – a specialist in selling Magic: The Gathering cards – has also had issues with Royal Mail items going missing. His business is also based in Bath and was affected over similar dates to Bath TCG’s.

“I realised it was theft when two customers in different parts of the country sent me pictures of their packages already open with the contents missing, within minutes of each other,” Stack said. “We’d previously had one sent to France turn up the same way a couple of weeks before, but I put it down to the buyer taking a bit of a chance that I’d have no way to hold them to account for pretending there had been an issue. In total we’ve had about £120-worth stolen so far – we had previously sent over 1,200 orders without any issues.”

Stack also halted online sales for a week, costing him £500 in revenue. Other sellers in the area have mentioned similar problems to him. Unfortunately, as most card businesses in the UK use CardMarket to sell online, it’s the buyer who picks the delivery method, and most often they use Royal Mail services. Cards are often sent in distinctive hard-backed envelopes to protect the contents, often with shop branding on stickers or seals.

Royal Mail is investigating the issue and liaising with the affected businesses. A spokesperson told the Guardian: “The safety and security of mail is a top priority and we take any reports of theft very seriously. We investigate concerns thoroughly and take action where necessary, including working with law enforcement.” Investigations are still ongoing; in the meantime, businesses must choose between risking theft and damaged reputation for their stores, or halting online sales and losing revenue.

With a new, highly sought-after 30th anniversary Pokémon card set due to release this month, retailers are already anticipating an increase in scalper and reselling activity, leading to even more potential for thieves to target those selling cards online. We asked the Pokémon Company for comment on how they’re dealing with increased demand and the rise in thefts, but they have yet to respond.

fullText:
US tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan police

Sadiq Khan has agreed for his text messages and emails to be searched as part of a legal battle with Palantir, the high court has been told, after he prevented the US technology company from working with the Metropolitan police.

The London mayor stepped in to block a £50m deal between Palantir and the Met in May, with the artificial intelligence developer suing Khan’s office over the decision.

Legal representatives for the mayor said they “did not originally consider it necessary” for Khan to be among those to have their communications searched before next year’s court case. But they relented, citing persistence from Palantir.

Sarah Brown, Khan’s former director of communications, who now works for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will also have her correspondence searched.

The proposed two-year deal would have allowed Palantir, which works for the Israeli military and the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, to provide AI technology to automate intelligence analysis in criminal investigations.

But the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac), which oversees large Scotland Yard contracts, said there had been a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules. It said police had seriously considered only one supplier (Palantir).

After the announcement, Palantir accused Khan of “putting politics above public safety” before declaring in June that it planned to sue the London mayor.

At a preliminary hearing on Thursday, the high court was told Khan and more than a dozen other Mopac and Greater London Authority officials would be classed as “custodians”.

The designation means their digital communications, including text messages, WhatsApp messages, and Microsoft Teams chats – insofar as they exist – will be searched for anything relevant to the issues in the legal tussle. These will then be disclosed to Palantir.

Joseph Barrett KC, for the mayor’s office, said in written submissions: “Mopac did not originally consider it necessary or proportionate for the mayor to be added as a custodian, given that the decision was taken by the deputy mayor for policing and crime; his senior position; and the likelihood that any documents held by him would be held by other individuals.

“However, Palantir has persisted in its requests, and Mopac has consented on a pragmatic basis.”

Brown, who in July moved from the mayor’s office to be appointed director of communications at Downing Street, was also listed as a custodian, meaning she too will have her correspondence searched, the court heard.

The decision to include Brown comes after Palantir said in court documents outlining its claim that press articles regarding the mayor’s office vetoing the Met deal cited concerns about Palantir’s values and ethics. Mopac has confirmed Brown “initiated” press briefings about the move.

The date range for the communication searches is still to be determined.

 Mopac reportedly is demanding to see Palantir’s own internal documents related to the deal, which the company is said to be resisting.

fullText:
Student protesters among those hacked, says digital rights group, though Aleksandar Vučić’s government denies spying

At least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier this year in what the digital rights group Share Foundation said was the largest documented ​wave of such infection in Serbia to date.

The wave of spyware infections was discovered in August after Apple notified people in 110 ⁠countries that they had probably been victims ⁠of mercenary spyware.

The Citizen Lab, which carries out forensic analyses of spyware attacks, released an analysis on Wednesday showing that at least one of the Serbians had been targeted with the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, which would have given the attacker “total access to the device”.

Share said those targeted included members of a Serbian student movement that has been a thorn in the side of the government of Aleksandar Vučić since 2024. Coalescing out of countrywide protests that followed the collapse of a train station that winter, it is one of the largest student movements in Europe.

Vučić has been in power for more than a decade, during which time critics have said he has overseen a hollowing-out of institutions while steering the country closer to Moscow.

There is no evidence that Vučić’s government was the entity that targeted the student with the Pegasus spyware. However, other spyware used against the students, including a software called NoviSpy, has been previously connected to Serbian authorities.

In an interview with Euronews Serbia TV on Wednesday, Ana Brnabić, the parliamentary speaker and a ranking member of the ruling Serbian Progressive party, denied that students had been spied on. “Absolutely not,” she said. “I do not believe a single word they’ve [students, Share] said.”

Share said the timing – during March’s local elections – may have been a practice run before snap elections set for this October.

“This is the largest documented wave of surveillance in Serbia so far,” said Andrijana Ristic, a policy adviser at Share. “We imagine … that the local elections were basically used as a test for the ruling party to see [the spyware’s] strengths, but also to see the amount of pressure they are able to exert over the students and the opposition.”

John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at the Citizen Lab, said: “Our forensic findings, and this fresh wave of Apple threat notifications reveal that Serbia’s peaceful pro-democracy movement is being aggressively targeted with mercenary spyware ahead of key 2026 election cycles.”

Milica Popović, one of the students who was targeted, called the attacks “cruel”. She said: “Thinking that someone may have entered my private space without my knowledge made me feel so exposed.”

But, she said, the attack, as uncomfortable as it was, would not deter her or the student movement. “If their intention was to frighten us, or make us stop, it will not work.”

NSO Group, which makes Pegasus, a spyware that has been leveraged by authoritarian states to target journalists, human rights campaigners and dissidents, began as an Israeli company with close ties to the military.

It is now under US ownership, and appears to be searching for a way into the US market, including through efforts to get off the US Commerce Department’s blacklist. However, this and other incidents will raise questions about what has been described as their attempt to rebrand as an “ethical spyware company”.

NSO Group has been permanently barred by a US court from targeting WhatsApp users and Meta products. It is unclear if this most recent Pegasus attack happened via WhatsApp.

“Today, Pegasus is still being used to hack people campaigning for democracy. NSO spent a decade promising reform, yet their spyware is still an instrument of political repression,” said Railton.

NSO Group was approached for comment.

US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyage
description: With military haircuts and moustaches, the US sailors stand out against the flip-flops of the usual Pattaya crowd.
fullText:
Far from hitting the bars and fleshpots of the Thai beach resort of Pattaya, in their first hours onshore most of the nearly 5,000 sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln seemed determined to go shopping.

At the Hard Rock Hotel – one of two beachside hotels where they were able to stay off the ship – they hung around clutching their recent purchases. But perhaps, after a record 250 days confined inside a grey steel warship, the normality of a trip to the mall might have been just what they needed.

With their military haircuts, moustaches and navy t-shirts, they stood out against the usual Pattaya crowd in flip-flops and beachwear.

Night, though, is when this resort city comes into its own, putting on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars.

Pattaya's tourism industry has been hit by conflict in the Middle East, where the USS Abraham Lincoln was last operating, with many of the tourists the city depends on choosing to stay at home.

Local establishments have been hoping American sailors, arriving with nine months of unspent salary while at sea, will provide a much-needed boost. On Wednesday night, the city's most famous promenade, Walking Street, was very much open to them, with a huge, illuminated sign at its entrance welcoming the crew of the US carrier.

They have, however, been reminded the sex industry is off-limits, as prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand.

But alcohol was flowing. By midnight some of the younger sailors were so inebriated they had to prop each other up. Others edged nervously into the red-lit caverns of the go-go bars, with their gyrating and barely-clothed pole dancers.

Conversation over the pounding music was challenging. One older crew member told us they really needed the break.

"The news says we've been at sea for nine months. To be honest I've lost track of time," he said.

"It got boring. It's never big enough on board. It's big but it still feels like a boat, especially when you're sharing it with thousands of people." How long would it take them to get home to California? "Too long," he said.

Restaurant owner Kosol Homkhunthod said the American sailors had "created a buzz" in town and among his staff - business had been "really slow" lately.

And a passing tourist described seeing "tonnes of people sitting on the beach", with soldiers in good spirits. "It's not like that every day."

But bar owner Kanta Saenkla complained many of the sailors appeared to simply be roaming around rather than enjoying the local bars.

"They haven't really come in for drinks or anything," she said. "Mostly they just walk around. They're not spending money like they did in previous years."

Out partying or not, Pattaya is a welcome respite for the crew.

Shakeira Fairfax, mother of 25-year-old sailor Jada Fairfax, told Reuters there had been moments over the past few months when "morale was low".

She described the period after hostilities broke out in the Middle East as an "uncertain" and "scary" time.

"I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'mum', I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," Fairfax added.

The crew have been well-drilled not to talk about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln during its long combat deployment in the operation against Iran, which have been the subject of criticism back in the US.

Some sailors were wary of making any conversation at all. Others referred journalists' questions to their media teams. Visible everywhere in Pattaya were the men wearing t-shirts emblazoned with the letters SLG, or Shore Liaison Group.

It is their job to maintain discipline on land, to watch out for the crew members, some of whom are very young and inexperienced, and to co-ordinate with the local authorities during port calls.

US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson did not answer questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing while in Pattaya, saying that "we're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can".

US personnel, he added, would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".

The decision by the USS Abraham Lincoln to stop in Pattaya makes a lot of sense. Port calls by the US Navy in Thailand, a long-standing treaty ally, are routine with well-established protocols.

It is also on the ship's route from the Gulf to California, giving the crew a chance to let off steam, and enjoy a break from the demands of life on board a warship.

If their stop in Thailand does the trick, any frustration they may feel over their unexpectedly long and tough mission may have dissipated by the time they get home.

title: Burning Man evicts Christian camp for breaking privacy rules
description: Camp "received multiple warnings and opportunities to correct their behavior, yet continued to violate our policies," Burning Man said.
fullText:
BLACK ROCK CITY, Nevada — Burning Man officials said they evicted a Christian-themed camp from the annual event here in the Nevada desert after the group repeatedly ignored rules about consent and photography.

Organizers of the "Shift the Atmosphere" complained on social media that they were targeted over their expressions of faith, which included preaching and on-site baptisms. But witnesses told the Reno Gazette-Journal, part of the USA TODAY Network, the group used aggressive tactics on both adults and children to share the gospel of Jesus.

In a statement, Burning Man officials said camp organizers were repeatedly warned to change their behavior. While the group complained online that their eviction violated Burning Man's principle of "radical inclusivity," Burning Man officials said the group violated another core tenet: privacy.

As a private, ticketed event, Burning Man's annual Black Rock City gathering is subject to strict privacy rules set by the organization. Those restrictions, which also apply to the media, include limiting photography and video, typically by requiring prior consent of anyone being filmed.

Longtime Burning Man attendees said they'd never seen an entire camp evicted during the event. Instead, specific attendees are usually removed, or camps not allowed back the next year.

"Burning Man takes participants' right to privacy seriously. Seeking permission and consent before filming or engaging other participants in Black Rock City is a requirement and responsibility for anyone at the event," Burning Man officials said in a Sept. 3 statement. "This camp received multiple warnings and opportunities to correct their behavior, yet continued to violate our policies and were therefore evicted."

Videos, confirmed by witnesses, showed a heavy law enforcement presence at the camp as participants dismantled tents and other structures at night in high winds. By daylight on Wednesday, Sept. 2, the camp was gone, leaving a blank space in the middle of the sprawling Burning Man encampment.

In a series of video statements posted online, camp organizer Calvin Hinerman said volunteer Black Rock Rangers and federal law enforcement forced the camp to pack up in the middle of the night. Witnesses said one of the tents blew into the road late at night, posing a safety hazard.

"We are being Kicked out of BURNING MAN for having faith in JESUS!?! So much for 'radical inclusion,'" Hinerman posted. In other videos, Hinerman and other camp attendees insisted they had permission from everyone they filmed.

The camp was set up across the street from Kidsville, a temporary Burning Man home to hundreds of children and their families. More than 1,000 children are attending this year's event.

In video posts leading up to the Aug. 30 official start of Burning Man, an event focused on community, free expression and the arts that draws tens of thousands of people, Hinerman showed off the camp's video wall and promised they would be playing Christian electronic dance music.

"What's going to happen is these people are going to come in and they're going to get hit with the glory of God," he said. "The presence of God is going to come upon them."

Hinerman later condemned Burning Man for allowing naked people to walk around in front of children.

Witnesses told the Reno Gazette-Journal the camp attracted attendees by offering coffee and matcha, and then tried to get people to accept Jesus as their savior. While some attendees said they brushed off the evangelizing, others said it felt aggressive for the otherwise almost-anything-goes event. While "radical inclusion" is part of the event's ethos, so is gifting without expectation or obligation.

Burning Man officials did not immediately comment on whether the camp's eviction was accompanied by trespassing charges.

title: Tim Cook stepped down as Apple CEO, but the ‘Trump whisperer’ isn’t going anywhere
description: Cook is giving up Apple’s top job, but his years navigating Trump, tariffs, and China are still valuable enough for the tech giant to keep him close.
fullText:
Tim Cook may be giving up Apple's top job, but the company isn't letting its longtime CEO fall far from the tree just yet.

Cook, who handed the CEO title to longtime hardware chief John Ternus on Tuesday, will stay on as executive chair for the tech company, earning an annual salary of $2 million effective Sept. 26. As chair, Cook will continue assisting with certain aspects of Apple, including "engaging with policymakers around the world," the company said in April when it announced his new role.

Why is Cook staying on as executive chair?

How did Tim Cook become Trump's 'whisperer'?

What manufacturing commitments has Apple made to the US?

What is Tim Cook's new role and compensation at Apple?

Part of the reason Cook may stay on at Apple is that during his 15-year tenure, he became a sort of "Trump whisperer" in navigating the company's relationship with the president. Cook earned the nickname for his ability to strike deals and keep things smooth with the president, as seen through both his tariff negotiations and this year's CEO transition.

Cook even said he'd continue to manage the company's relationship with not only Trump but also the Chinese government, according to Bloomberg. Those relationships have become increasingly important to Apple as its sprawling Asian supply chain puts the company in the middle of Trump's push to use tariffs to bring more manufacturing to the U.S.—and leaves it navigating tensions between Washington and Beijing.

His package won't be limited to the $2 million annual comp either; he was approved for an equity award with a target value of $45 million, according to a regulatory filing.

Cook leaves the CEO job after 15 years at Apple's helm, having taken over shortly before cofounder Steve Jobs' death in 2011. During his tenure, Apple's market capitalization grew from roughly $347 billion to $4.6 trillion, all while increasingly navigating government issues, alongside product and operational challenges.

Cook figured out relatively early how to get Trump's ear.

"He's the one that calls me," Trump told reporters in 2019 when he was asked why he had a good relationship with Cook compared with other tech executives. At the time, tariffs were a problem. Trump said Cook had argued that levies on Apple's China-made products could put the company at a disadvantage against South Korean rival Samsung.

That relationship would be tested again after Trump returned to the White House. In February 2025, Apple announced it would spend $500 billion in the U.S. over four years, including plans to hire 20,000 workers.

But Cook's access to Trump did not mean Apple always got what it wanted. By May 2025, Trump was publicly criticizing Apple as the company expanded iPhone production in India, as part of its efforts to reduce its reliance on China.

title: 104-mph BMW crash in Malibu killed 4 sorority sisters. Was it murder?
description: Twenty-two-year-old Fraser Bohm was driving up to 104 mph when he lost control of his BMW and caused a crash that killed four Pepperdine University students.
fullText:
It was 8:30 p.m. on a Tuesday night and 22-year-old Fraser Bohm had just accidentally killed four sorority sisters.

Bohm was speeding in his BMW on Dead Man's Curve, a notorious stretch of Southern California's Pacific Coast Highway. Prosecutors say Bohm was driving 104 mph in a 45 mph zone when he lost control of the BMW and slammed into parked cars, which then barreled into the sorority sisters as they stood on a sidewalk on Oct. 17, 2023.

The crash killed Niamh Rolston, Peyton Stewart, Asha Weir and Deslyn Williams, all seniors at Pepperdine University in Malibu and members of the Alpha Phi sorority.

"I feel awful," Bohm told investigating officers, according to a transcript obtained by USA TODAY. "Trust me, I'm so (expletive) up."

Bohm did not set out to kill the young women that terrible night but he's being tried on four counts of second-degree murder and four counts of vehicular manslaughter at his upcoming trial on Dec. 1. Prosecutors argue that Bohm understood that driving so fast could have deadly consequences and did it anyway, showing "a reckless disregard for life."

Bohm's attorneys are arguing that a road rage driver clipped him just before the accident and point to his lack of criminal record or traffic violations.

"It was an accident, period," Bohm's high-profile attorney, Alan Jackson, told USA TODAY. "There was no malice in Fraser's heart. He meant no harm to anybody. He was reacting to circumstances that were outside his control and an accident occurred."

He added: "The DA's office has wildly overcharged this case."

If convicted of the murder charges, the now-24-year-old Bohm could spend the rest of his life in prison. If a jury finds him guilty of only the vehicular manslaughter charges, he could face as little as two years behind bars.

Bohm's trial is being closely watched for the questions it raises about what justice means for someone who doesn't intend to kill but whose actions have deadly consequences. The verdict against Bohm could also have implications for other similar cases in the future.

Though historically rare, murder or homicide charges in high-speed crashes that don't involve drugs or alcohol are becoming increasingly common, according to experts interviewed by USA TODAY. From Minnesota and Indiana to California and Florida, people across the nation who killed others while speeding are now facing charges that carry life sentences.

"Everything seems like a murder," said Jonathan Cherney, a former longtime detective who investigated fatal crashes for Southern California's Irvine Police Department. He now does accident reconstruction for both prosecutors and defense attorneys nationwide as an independent consultant.

"I have so many cases," Cherney said, "I can't even accept new ones."

As Bohm's trial approaches, USA TODAY is looking closer at the crash, what led up to it, and the central question facing jurors: Did Fraser Bohm make a terrible mistake or did he commit murder?

The 4 sorority sisters killed in crash: They left a 'legacy of goodness'

At about 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 17, 2023, Fraser Bohm had just picked up an order of tacos and was driving up the Pacific Coast Highway in Malibu to meet friends, according to court records obtained by USA TODAY. Bohm, a college baseball prosect who lived in a $2.5 million Malibu home with his mother at the time, was driving the 2016 BMW that his parents gave him shortly before they filed for divorce in 2017, court records show.

Accounts vary wildly about what led up to the crash. While prosecutors have described Bohm as acting out of "complete and reckless disregard" for the lives of others, his attorneys have always asserted that Bohm crashed while fleeing from an aggressive road rage driver. The man Bohm identified as the other driver, Victor Calandra, has previously testified that he saw Bohm driving erratically and thought the 22-year-old was texting when he caught up to him at a stoplight.

"Hey, you need to be careful, you're going to hurt yourself," Calandra testified that he told Bohm just before the young man floored the gas pedal and crashed seconds later, according to the Pepperdine Graphic, the university newspaper that has closely been following the case.

Bohm's previous and current attorneys have given varied accounts about whether he was texting just before the crash. Bohm, described as being dazed from the crash, told police that he "must have been texting" but didn't remember. Bohm's attorney at the time, Michael Kraut, told reporters that Bohm was texting a friend at the stop light "and the guy next to him began to become irate."

"That person then gave chase to my client," Kraut said in 2023, according to CBS News. "My client continued at a regular speed … and then the other person came in his lane and started pushing him. That person then made contact with my client's car."

Kraut said Bohm wasn't going any faster than 70 mph and had only accelerated because he was "being chased." Bohm's current attorneys deny that he was texting, citing an independent cellphone analysis.

Seconds after the crash, Bohm told police that Calandra pulled him out of his BMW by the neck and "pretty much threatened to kill me," according to court records obtained by USA TODAY.

"He was like, 'You don't understand what you just did. Like, you crashed into all these people,'" Bohm told police.

Bohm told police that Calandra drove into his lane, causing him to swerve. He didn't mention road rage or being afraid during the interview but said he also didn't remember exactly what happened.

"I had to swerve ... And then I was already − I was going fast and then I slammed in front of ... it was two other cars," he said. "I believe it was also just a blur because my airbags had went off. So I didn't see anything ... I really wish I could hone down and understand what had happened."

Whether Bohm was going 70 or 104 mph − or somewhere in between − Rolston, Stewart, Weir and Williams never stood a chance. The young women, who were all 20 and 21, died instantly, shattering their loved ones and the close-knit community at Pepperdine, a Christian school with about 9,000 students whose picturesque campus overlooks the Pacific Ocean.

Police initially booked Bohm on manslaughter charges but they arrested him a week later on the murder counts. Bohm has been out awaiting trial after his family posted $4 million bail.

In order for the prosecutors in Bohm's trial to get a murder conviction, they don't have to prove he intended to kill anyone. They have to show that he had "implied malice," meaning that even though he knew that driving so fast could kill people, he did it anyway, according to California law.

Prosecutors could draw on Bohm's own words to sway jurors. At the scene of the crash, police asked Bohm whether he was familiar with the phrase "speed kills." Bohm replied that he was and that it means a lot to him because two of his friends died in a high-speed crash, according to a transcript of the interview obtained by USA TODAY.

Bohm cited a 2020 crash that killed 20-year-old driver Ezekial Bishop and his passenger, 18-year-old Ryan Breaux, recording artist Frank Ocean's little brother. Bishop was driving drunk at speeds of 138 mph in his Tesla when he lost control of the car and hit a tree in the suburban Los Angeles city of Thousand Oaks, according to a police report obtained by USA TODAY.

"They were going way, way, way too fast," Bohm told police after his own crash. "Those are my two best friends. I know all about that stuff ... I never got closure for what happened with them."

Prosecutors also argue that because Bohm lived in the area and drove there all the time, he knew just how dangerous it was to drive so fast. Along many stretches of the Pacific Coast Highway in Malibu, the roadway is lined with homes and businesses, with speed limits of 45 mph.

"The defendant knew it is not the Autobahn," prosecutors argue in court records. "Specifically, that stretch of PCH is where people live, drive, walk to restaurants, turn in and out of their driveways, parallel park. ... That area is teeming with human life. The defendant knew that."

Bohm's high-profile defense team (who replaced Kraut last year) will have to prove to jurors that Bohm did not know his behavior was likely to result in death.

The defense team is led by attorney Alan Jackson, who previously represented Nick Reiner in the murder case involving his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner. He also has represented actor Kevin Spacey, producer Harvey Weinstein, and he spent about two years in Massachusetts, representing the since-acquitted Karen Read in a murder case that gripped the nation.

Jackson told USA TODAY that everyone should be troubled by Bohm's case if the prosecution's strongest piece of evidence is that his client acknowledged being familiar with the phrase "speed kills."

"That phrase is a desperate attempt to hang something around Fraser's neck that doesn't exist," Jackson said. "There is no person in the last 30 years who has a driver's license in this country who hasn't heart the phrase 'speed kills.'"

If that's the predicate for a murder charge these days, he said, then every crash involving speed and a fatality could be charged as murder.

"Be careful what you wish for," he said. "What they've got to prove is that at that moment Fraser was in that car in the seconds before this tragic accident was that he had a murderous mind. If they can't prove that they can't prove murder."

Jackson has twice asked the judge in Bohm's case to throw out the murder charges, arguing in court that "implied malice murder requires more than just tragedy and danger."

"Speed is not malice," Jackson said last year, arguing that Bohm has no criminal record, no history of speeding, and that he wasn't impaired, racing, or texting.

Both times, the judge denied Jackson's request to throw out the murder charges against Bohm.

Jackson also has argued in recent court documents that Bohm couldn't have expected the crash to happen.

Though speeding is a well-documented problem along the Pacific Coast Highway, Bohm's was the only fatal crash of 179 collisions that occurred on the same .8-mile stretch of road over the course of more than 10 years, Jackson argued, citing California Highway Patrol data.

Even if Bohm reached 104 mph, that alone wasn't "highly probable to result in death," Jackson's team argued in court records last month. "It was instead a regular occurrence on this roadway that had never before produced a fatal outcome."

Bohm's trial had been set to start on Sept. 8, but the judge in the case recently agreed to postpone it until Dec. 1. The delay came after Jackson said during a Sept. 2 court hearing that his team would need more time to prepare for the prosecution's plan to introduce evidence that a nitrous oxygen can was found in Bohm's car at the crash scene.

Jackson said he expressed concern that it was turning into a DUI case, but prosecutors assured the court that they are not trying to prove that Bohm was high, just that he was distracted.

Murder charges involving fatal crashes are a relatively recent phenomenon that is gaining in popularity among prosecutors in California and beyond, according to experts who spoke to USA TODAY.

In California, they're known as Watson murders, named for a 1981 state Supreme Court case finding that second-degree murder charges were appropriate for a man named Robert Watson, who was drunk and driving at speeds of 84 mph in a 35 mph zone when he hit another car, killing a woman and her 6-year-old daughter in Redding in northern California.

Though the case set a precedent that implied malice could be applied to unintentional car crashes, it wasn't until 2008 that prosecutors began filing a significant number of such cases, said Cherney, the former police detective who now does accident reconstruction for defense and prosecution teams across the nation.

That year, the Orange County District Attorney's Office in Southern California created the first vehicular homicide unit in the state and one of the first in the nation. In the beginning, the team largely focused on fatal drunk-driving cases, Cherney said. Over time, other prosecutor's offices created their own units and began cracking down on fatal crashes involving egregious circumstances, like excessive speed, he said.

Cut to today, and more prosecutors than ever are pursuing murder charges in such cases, according to Cherney and Dan McLain, a former detective who investigates car crashes for the Orange County Sheriff's Office and now is an accident reconstructionist for both defense and prosecution teams in California.

Driving the increase in murder charges in fatal crashes are a few factors, Cherney and McClain agree. Among them: better technology that can prove someone was driving dangerously, and sometimes, politics.

"The DA's office is obviously very political," Cherney said. "A lot of times, prosecutors are pressured by what the family thinks, and more than one DA has said to me, 'I would rather take this trial and lose then tell the family I'm not going to file it.'"

A number of murder cases involving dangerous driving have made national headlines in recent months and years.

In Florida in July, prosecutors announced second-degree murder charges against Marquavious Wheaton, who they say was driving up to 115 mph in his BMW just north of Orlando before he broadsided an SUV and killed the two brothers inside, 42-year-old Christopher Marier and 40-year-old Tyler Marier.

In a news release about the case, prosecutors said they are seeking life in prison for Wheaton and that his actions "revealed a depraved mind and a corrupt disregard for the lives and safety of others." Wheaton has pleaded not guilty.

In Minneapolis last year, a jury found then-25-year-old Derrick Thompson guilty of five counts of third-degree murder and 10 counts of criminal vehicular homicide for speeding at about 100 mph, running a red light and causing a crash that killed five young women between the ages of 17 and 20 who were preparing for a wedding. Thompson, who is the son of a former state lawmaker, was sentenced to 58 years in prison.

In Arizona last year, 35-year-old Robb Hintzsche pleaded no contest to two counts of second-degree murder in a crash that killed a Lyft driver, her passenger and the passenger's dog in the Phoenix suburb of Gilbert. Authorities say he was driving drunk and going up to 96 mph in a 45-mph zone, ran a red light and crashed into the Lyft car, killing the two women and pet inside. A judge sentenced him to 24 years in prison.

In a notorious case in the Los Angeles area, a jury found then-60-year-old Rebecca Grossman guilty in 2024 of two counts of second-degree murder and other charges in a hit-and-run crash that killed two brothers who were 8 and 11 years old. Authorities say that Grossman was driving drunk and going 81 mph in a 45-mph zone in her Mercedes-Benz SUV when she slammed into the brothers, who were in a crosswalk with their parents and other family in the suburb of Westlake Village. Grossman was sentenced to 15 years to life in prison.

But not all cases are leading to convictions. On Wednesday, Aug. 2, a Southern California jury found 38-year-old Jim Rosado not guilty of second-degree murder in a high-speed 2021 crash that killed his 18-year-old niece in Irvine, about 50 miles southeast of Los Angeles.

Though Rosado tested positive for a small amount of meth and had been going up to 90 mph, the evidence indicated that Rosado had fallen asleep and that his car drifted off the freeway before hitting a guardrail, Cherney said. The jury did convict Rosado of driving under the influence and he was sentenced to five years in prison, but Rosado has been behind bars on a $2 million bail since 2021 so won't have to serve any additional time.

At Bohm's murder trial, McLain said that prosecutors will have a strong case if they can convince jurors that he was driving at 104 mph and if they are swayed by his comments about knowing that speed kills.

"I think that all played a factor in prosecutors saying, 'We want to throw the book at this guy to teach him and everybody a lesson,'" McClain said. "'Lets get the word out. If you're doing 104 in a 45 and kill four people, you're going to spend at least 60 years in prison, if not your entire life.'"

Jackson told USA TODAY that he's been troubled by his client's portrayal in some news media outlets as "some spoiled rich Malibu kid" and said that Bohm is just "a normal young man."

"He's quiet, he's circumspect, he's focused on athletics and academics and he was heading toward college to play baseball," he said. "He had nothing but the brightest stars in his future, as did the young ladies who lost their lives that night."

He continued to say that some have grasped onto the idea of Bohm's "upper-middle class" upbringing "as if that's some indicator that there was some intention here, or that he just didn't care about human life."

"None of that is true," Jackson continued. "He is deeply, deeply affected by this, as you can imagine. He will live in the prison of his own memory of what happened that night for the rest of his life."

Jackson said he is in no way diminishing the tragic loss of life in the case, but that "in world of 8 billion people, sometimes accidents happen."

"This is not a murder case," he added. "This has never been a murder case."

Contributing: Melina Khan, USA TODAY

Amanda Lee Myers is a senior crime reporter who covers the death penalty, cold case investigations, breaking news for USA TODAY. Follow her on X at @amandaleeusat.

title: Putin cites chance of peace deal, Zelenskiy says US negotiators to visit both countries
description: VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zel...
fullText:
VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said U.S. negotiators trying to broker a deal would ‌soon visit both Moscow and Kyiv.

Putin, speaking at an economic forum in Russia's far east, said a number of countries including the U.S. ‌and China were ready to support a peace settlement.

"Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine," he said.

"We are grateful to everyone ​attempting to contribute to a settlement. Is there a chance? In my view, yes, there is."

In Kyiv, Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address that preliminary dates had been set for a visit by U.S. negotiators.

"We expect to see representatives of the U.S. president here in Kyiv," Zelenskiy said.

"There will be a meeting with them in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are expecting a meeting with them in the coming days. It is very important. It is important that America ‌continues to be active."

In Washington, U.S. President Donald Trump ⁠said he wanted to see an end to the war and losses sustained by both sides.

"I just want to see that end. I think we'll get it," Trump told GB News in an interview that aired on Thursday, a day ⁠after telling reporters he wanted a summit with Putin when the Kremlin leader is ready for a peace deal.

After 4-1/2 years of Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two, it is rare for either side to offer an upbeat assessment of peace prospects. They last met for U.S.-mediated talks in February.

Since then, with the U.S. ​distracted by ​the Iran war, both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up long-range air attacks deep ​inside the other's territory. Hostilities at sea have escalated sharply ‌with attacks by both sides on ports and commercial shipping, pushing up global grain prices.

U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded the effort to broker an agreement, were last in Moscow in January. They have yet to visit Kyiv.

Chicago wheat futures dropped by more than 2% on Putin's comments.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had earlier told reporters in Kyiv that he saw a "new dynamic" coming in peace efforts, with more active political and diplomatic engagement.

Neither side, however, gave reasons to expect progress.

On the contrary, the Kremlin leader said Ukraine's latest actions presented an obstacle.

In response to a question, Putin ‌said Ukrainian attacks on civilian merchant ships and "reported threats of attacks on civilian aircraft" ​were "acts of state terrorism", which he said "complicates the prospects for bilateral peace talks".

Zelenskiy warned airlines ​and insurance companies this week that the presence of Ukrainian drones had ​made Russian skies dangerous, although he said Ukraine would target only Russian military facilities and not threaten civilian aircraft.

On ‌Wednesday, Ukraine urged the U.N.'s aviation agency to ask members to ​ban operations in Russian airspace. Ukraine ​has been cut off from international civil aviation because its own airspace is considered unsafe since Russia invaded in 2022.

PUTIN: CONTACTS MOSTLY TAKE PLACE VIA INTELLIGENCE AGENCIES

Putin said contacts with Ukraine were still taking place.

"It is difficult for me to say right now to what extent these ​contacts are leading to a peace agreement, given ‌the statements we have heard recently from Ukraine's top leadership," he said.

"However, contacts do exist and are continuing on an ongoing basis - ​gain, primarily through intelligence channels."

(Additional reporting by Reuters in Moscow, Max Hunder in Kyiv, Anna Pruchnicka in Gdansk and Tabahriti, Sam ​in London); Writing by Mark Trevelyan; Editing by Andrew Heavens and David Gregorio)

fullText:
OTTAWA, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday his government was ready to sign a trade deal ‌with the U.S. that benefits both countries, adding any agreement would ‌need to have stability and credibility.
